# Load required package
library(powerSurvEpi)

# Study parameters
n_per_group <- 200
hazard_ratio <- 0.7
event_prob_treatment <- 0.3707
event_prob_control <- 0.4890
alpha <- 0.05
two_sided <- TRUE

# Calculate power using powerCT.default
# powerCT.default expects:
# - n: number of subjects per group (equal allocation)
# - lambda0: event rate in control
# - lambda1: event rate in treatment  
# - rho: hazard ratio (treatment/control)
# - alpha: type I error
# - power: NULL (we want to calculate it)
# - sided: 1 for one-sided, 2 for two-sided

# From event probabilities, we derive event rates
# The event probability under constant hazard rate is related to the follow-up time
# However, for Freedman's approximation, we can use the event counts directly
# Expected number of events in each group:
n_events_control <- n_per_group * event_prob_control
n_events_treatment <- n_per_group * event_prob_treatment

cat("Study parameters:\n")
cat("Sample size per group:", n_per_group, "\n")
cat("Hazard ratio (treatment/control):", hazard_ratio, "\n")
cat("Event probability (treatment):", event_prob_treatment, "\n")
cat("Event probability (control):", event_prob_control, "\n")
cat("Expected number of events (treatment):", n_events_treatment, "\n")
cat("Expected number of events (control):", n_events_control, "\n")
cat("Total expected events:", n_events_treatment + n_events_control, "\n\n")

# powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default uses the Freedman approach
# It requires event rates (lambda) rather than event probabilities
# We interpret the event probabilities as the proportion of participants experiencing the event
# For constant hazard rate: event_prob = 1 - exp(-lambda * tau)
# Solving for lambda: lambda = -log(1 - event_prob) / tau
# But if we set tau = 1 (unit time), then lambda = -log(1 - event_prob)

lambda0 <- -log(1 - event_prob_control)
lambda1 <- -log(1 - event_prob_treatment)

cat("Derived event rates (assuming unit follow-up time):\n")
cat("Control event rate (lambda0):", lambda0, "\n")
cat("Treatment event rate (lambda1):", lambda1, "\n")
cat("Ratio of rates (lambda1/lambda0):", lambda1/lambda0, "\n\n")

# Calculate power using powerCT.default
power_result <- powerCT.default(
  n = n_per_group,
  lambda0 = lambda0,
  lambda1 = lambda1,
  rho = hazard_ratio,
  alpha = alpha,
  power = NULL,
  sided = 2
)

cat("Power calculation via powerCT.default:\n")
cat("Power:", power_result$power, "\n")
cat("Calculation details:\n")
print(power_result)

# Store result for output
power_value <- power_result$power

# Emit structured result
cat("\n=== RESULT ===\n")
cat("Method: Freedman approximation via powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default\n")
cat("Power:", power_value, "\n")
cat("Two-sided alpha:", alpha, "\n")
cat("Sample size per group:", n_per_group, "\n")

     was proposed by Freedman (1982).

     experimental group (E) and a control group (C) in a clinical trial
     with a maximum follow-up of t years.  The Cox proportional hazards
     regression model is assumed to have the form:

# Load required package
library(powerSurvEpi)

# Parameters
n_per_group <- 200
hr <- 0.7
p_treatment <- 0.3707
p_control <- 0.4890
alpha <- 0.05
two_sided <- TRUE

# The Freedman approximation requires hazard rates, not event probabilities directly.
# However, powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default expects parameters:
# - n: number of subjects per group
# - lambda0: event rate in control group
# - lambda1: event rate in treatment group (or HR relating to control)
# - alpha: significance level
# - power: if NULL, calculate power

# For the Freedman approximation with event probabilities, we need to interpret these
# as proportions of events. The hazard ratio of 0.7 means treatment has 0.7 times the
# hazard rate of control.

# Using powerSurvEpi::powerCT with specified parameters
result <- powerSurvEpi::powerCT(
  n = n_per_group,
  lambda0 = p_control,  # Event rate in control
  lambda1 = p_treatment,  # Event rate in treatment
  alpha = alpha,
  power = NULL,
  alternative = "two.sided"
)

# Extract power
power_value <- result$power

cat("Power Calculation using Freedman Approximation\n")
cat("==============================================\n")
cat("Method: powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default\n")
cat("Approximation: Freedman\n")
cat("Test: Two-sided log-rank\n")

cat("  Test direction: Two-sided\n")
cat("  Allocation: 1:1\n")

cat("  Power: ", power_value, "\n")

POWER_AGENT_RESULT = list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "power",
      value = power_value,

    )
  )
)

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     Power calculation for the Comparison of Survival Curves Between
     Two Groups under the Cox Proportional-Hazards Model for clinical
     trials. Some parameters will be estimated based on a pilot data
     set.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     powerCT(formula, 
             dat, 
             nE, 
             nC, 
             RR, 
             alpha = 0.05)
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

 formula: A formula object, e.g. ‘Surv(time, status) ~ x’, where ‘time’
          is a vector of survival/censoring time, ‘status’ is a vector
          of censoring indicator, ‘x’ is the group indicator, which is
          a factor object in R and takes only two possible values (‘C’
          for control group and ‘E’ for experimental group). See also
          the documentation of the function ‘survfit’ in the library
          ‘survival’.

     dat: a data frame representing the pilot data set and containing
          at least 3 columns: (1) survival/censoring time; (2)
          censoring indicator; (3) group indicator which is a factor
          object in R and takes only two possible values (‘C’ for
          control group and ‘E’ for experimental group).

      nE: integer. number of participants in the experimental group.

      nC: integer. number of participants in the control group.

      RR: numeric. postulated hazard ratio.

   alpha: numeric. type I error rate.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     This is an implementation of the power calculation method
     described in Section 14.12 (page 807) of Rosner (2006). The method
     was proposed by Freedman (1982).

     The movitation of this function is that some times we do not have
     information about m or p_E and p_C available, but we have a pilot
     data set that can be used to estimate p_E and p_C hence m, where
     m=n_E p_E + n_C p_C is the expected total number of events over
     both groups, n_E and n_C are numbers of participants in group E
     (experimental group) and group C (control group), respectively.
     p_E is the probability of failure in group E (experimental group)
     over the maximum time period of the study (t years).  p_C is the
     probability of failure in group C (control group) over the maximum
     time period of the study (t years).

     Suppose we want to compare the survival curves between an
     experimental group (E) and a control group (C) in a clinical trial
     with a maximum follow-up of t years.  The Cox proportional hazards
     regression model is assumed to have the form:

                      h(t|X_1)=h_0(t)\exp(beta_1 X_1).                  
     
     Let n_E be the number of participants in the E group and n_C be
     the number of participants in the C group.  We wish to test the
     hypothesis H0: RR=1 versus H1: RR not equal to 1, where
     RR=\exp(beta_1)=underlying hazard ratio for the E group versus the
     C group. Let RR be the postulated hazard ratio, alpha be the
     significance level. Assume that the test is a two-sided test. If
     the ratio of participants in group E compared to group C =
     n_E/n_C=k, then the power of the test is

             power=Phi(sqrt{k*m}*|RR-1|/(k*RR+1)-z_{1-alpha/2}),        
     
     where

                             m=n_E p_E+n_C p_C,                         
     
     and z_{1-alpha/2} is the 100 (1-alpha/2)-th percentile of the
     standard normal distribution N(0, 1), Phi is the cumulative
     distribution function (CDF) of N(0, 1).

     p_C and p_E can be calculated from the following formulaes:

                 p_C=sum_{i=1}^{t}D_i, p_E=sum_{i=1}^{t}E_i,            
     
     where D_i=lambda_i A_i C_i, E_i=RRlambda_i B_i C_i,
     A_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-lambda_j),
     B_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-RRlambda_j),
     C_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-delta_j).  And lambda_i is the probability
     of failure at time ‘i’ among participants in the control group,
     given that a participant has survived to time i-1 and is not
     censored at time i-1, i.e., the approximate hazard time i in the
     control group, i=1,...,t; RRlambda_i is the probability of failure
     at time ‘i’ among participants in the experimental group, given
     that a participant has survived to time i-1 and is not censored at
     time i-1, i.e., the approximate hazard time i in the experimental
     group, i=1,...,t; delta is the prbability that a participant is
     censored at time i given that he was followed up to time i and has
     not failed, i=0, 1, ..., t, which is assumed the same in each
     group.

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

mat.lambda: a matrix with 9 columns and ‘nTimes+1’ rows, where ‘nTimes’
          is the number of observed time points for the control group
          in the data set. The 9 columns are (1) ‘time’ - observed time
          point for the control group; (2) ‘lambda’; (3) ‘RRlambda’;
          (4) ‘delta’; (5) ‘A’; (6) ‘B’; (7) ‘C’; (8) ‘D’; (9) ‘E’.
          Please refer to the Details section for the definitions of
          elements of these quantities. See also Table 14.24 on page
          809 of Rosner (2006).

mat.event: a matrix with 5 columns and ‘nTimes+1’ rows, where ‘nTimes’
          is the number of observed time points for control group in
          the data set. The 5 columns are (1) ‘time’ - observed time
          point for the control group; (2) ‘nEvent.C’ - number of
          events in the control group at each time point; (3)
          ‘nCensored.C’ - number of censorings in the control group at
          each time point; (4) ‘nSurvive.C’ - number of alived in the
          control group at each time point; (5) ‘nRisk.C’ - number of
          participants at risk in the control group at each time point.
          Please refer to Table 14.12 on page 787 of Rosner (2006).

      pC: estimated probability of failure in group C (control group)
          over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      pE: estimated probability of failure in group E (experimental
          group) over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

   power: the power of the test.

_ N_ o_ t_ e:

     (1) The estimates of RRlambda_i=RR*lambda_i. That is, ‘RRlambda’
     is not directly estimated based on data from the experimental
     group; (2) The power formula assumes that the central-limit
     theorem is valid and hence is appropriate for large samples.

_ R_ e_ f_ e_ r_ e_ n_ c_ e_ s:

# Load required package
library(powerSurvEpi)

# Parameters
n_per_group <- 200
hr <- 0.7
p_treatment <- 0.3707
p_control <- 0.4890
alpha <- 0.05
two_sided <- TRUE

# The Freedman approximation requires hazard rates, not event probabilities directly.
# However, powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default expects parameters:
# - n: number of subjects per group
# - lambda0: event rate in control group
# - lambda1: event rate in treatment group (or HR relating to control)
# - alpha: significance level
# - power: if NULL, calculate power

# For the Freedman approximation with event probabilities, we need to interpret these
# as proportions of events. The hazard ratio of 0.7 means treatment has 0.7 times the
# hazard rate of control.

# Using powerSurvEpi::powerCT with specified parameters
result <- powerSurvEpi::powerCT(
  n = n_per_group,
  lambda0 = p_control,  # Event rate in control
  lambda1 = p_treatment,  # Event rate in treatment
  alpha = alpha,
  power = NULL,
  alternative = "two.sided"
)

# Extract power
power_value <- result$power

cat("Power Calculation using Freedman Approximation\n")
cat("==============================================\n")
cat("Method: powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default\n")
cat("Approximation: Freedman\n")
cat("Test: Two-sided log-rank\n")
cat("\nInput Parameters:\n")
cat("  Participants per group (n): ", n_per_group, "\n")
cat("  Event probability in treatment: ", p_treatment, "\n")
cat("  Event probability in control: ", p_control, "\n")
cat("  Hazard ratio (HR): ", hr, "\n")
cat("  Significance level (alpha): ", alpha, "\n")
cat("  Test direction: Two-sided\n")
cat("  Allocation: 1:1\n")
cat("\nResult:\n")
cat("  Power: ", power_value, "\n")

POWER_AGENT_RESULT = list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "power",
      value = power_value,
      unit = "probability"
    )
  )
)

cat("\n")
print(jsonlite::toJSON(POWER_AGENT_RESULT, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     Power calculation for the Comparison of Survival Curves Between
     Two Groups under the Cox Proportional-Hazards Model for clinical
     trials. Some parameters will be estimated based on a pilot data
     set.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     powerCT(formula, 
             dat, 
             nE, 
             nC, 
             RR, 
             alpha = 0.05)
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

 formula: A formula object, e.g. ‘Surv(time, status) ~ x’, where ‘time’
          is a vector of survival/censoring time, ‘status’ is a vector
          of censoring indicator, ‘x’ is the group indicator, which is
          a factor object in R and takes only two possible values (‘C’
          for control group and ‘E’ for experimental group). See also
          the documentation of the function ‘survfit’ in the library
          ‘survival’.

     dat: a data frame representing the pilot data set and containing
          at least 3 columns: (1) survival/censoring time; (2)
          censoring indicator; (3) group indicator which is a factor
          object in R and takes only two possible values (‘C’ for
          control group and ‘E’ for experimental group).

      nE: integer. number of participants in the experimental group.

      nC: integer. number of participants in the control group.

      RR: numeric. postulated hazard ratio.

   alpha: numeric. type I error rate.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     This is an implementation of the power calculation method
     described in Section 14.12 (page 807) of Rosner (2006). The method
     was proposed by Freedman (1982).

     The movitation of this function is that some times we do not have
     information about m or p_E and p_C available, but we have a pilot
     data set that can be used to estimate p_E and p_C hence m, where
     m=n_E p_E + n_C p_C is the expected total number of events over
     both groups, n_E and n_C are numbers of participants in group E
     (experimental group) and group C (control group), respectively.
     p_E is the probability of failure in group E (experimental group)
     over the maximum time period of the study (t years).  p_C is the
     probability of failure in group C (control group) over the maximum
     time period of the study (t years).

     Suppose we want to compare the survival curves between an
     experimental group (E) and a control group (C) in a clinical trial
     with a maximum follow-up of t years.  The Cox proportional hazards
     regression model is assumed to have the form:

                      h(t|X_1)=h_0(t)\exp(beta_1 X_1).                  
     
     Let n_E be the number of participants in the E group and n_C be
     the number of participants in the C group.  We wish to test the
     hypothesis H0: RR=1 versus H1: RR not equal to 1, where
     RR=\exp(beta_1)=underlying hazard ratio for the E group versus the
     C group. Let RR be the postulated hazard ratio, alpha be the
     significance level. Assume that the test is a two-sided test. If
     the ratio of participants in group E compared to group C =
     n_E/n_C=k, then the power of the test is

             power=Phi(sqrt{k*m}*|RR-1|/(k*RR+1)-z_{1-alpha/2}),        
     
     where

                             m=n_E p_E+n_C p_C,                         
     
     and z_{1-alpha/2} is the 100 (1-alpha/2)-th percentile of the
     standard normal distribution N(0, 1), Phi is the cumulative
     distribution function (CDF) of N(0, 1).

     p_C and p_E can be calculated from the following formulaes:

                 p_C=sum_{i=1}^{t}D_i, p_E=sum_{i=1}^{t}E_i,            
     
     where D_i=lambda_i A_i C_i, E_i=RRlambda_i B_i C_i,
     A_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-lambda_j),
     B_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-RRlambda_j),
     C_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-delta_j).  And lambda_i is the probability
     of failure at time ‘i’ among participants in the control group,
     given that a participant has survived to time i-1 and is not
     censored at time i-1, i.e., the approximate hazard time i in the
     control group, i=1,...,t; RRlambda_i is the probability of failure
     at time ‘i’ among participants in the experimental group, given
     that a participant has survived to time i-1 and is not censored at
     time i-1, i.e., the approximate hazard time i in the experimental
     group, i=1,...,t; delta is the prbability that a participant is
     censored at time i given that he was followed up to time i and has
     not failed, i=0, 1, ..., t, which is assumed the same in each
     group.

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

mat.lambda: a matrix with 9 columns and ‘nTimes+1’ rows, where ‘nTimes’
          is the number of observed time points for the control group
          in the data set. The 9 columns are (1) ‘time’ - observed time
          point for the control group; (2) ‘lambda’; (3) ‘RRlambda’;
          (4) ‘delta’; (5) ‘A’; (6) ‘B’; (7) ‘C’; (8) ‘D’; (9) ‘E’.
          Please refer to the Details section for the definitions of
          elements of these quantities. See also Table 14.24 on page
          809 of Rosner (2006).

mat.event: a matrix with 5 columns and ‘nTimes+1’ rows, where ‘nTimes’
          is the number of observed time points for control group in
          the data set. The 5 columns are (1) ‘time’ - observed time
          point for the control group; (2) ‘nEvent.C’ - number of
          events in the control group at each time point; (3)
          ‘nCensored.C’ - number of censorings in the control group at
          each time point; (4) ‘nSurvive.C’ - number of alived in the
          control group at each time point; (5) ‘nRisk.C’ - number of
          participants at risk in the control group at each time point.
          Please refer to Table 14.12 on page 787 of Rosner (2006).

      pC: estimated probability of failure in group C (control group)
          over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      pE: estimated probability of failure in group E (experimental
          group) over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

   power: the power of the test.

_ N_ o_ t_ e:

     (1) The estimates of RRlambda_i=RR*lambda_i. That is, ‘RRlambda’
     is not directly estimated based on data from the experimental
     group; (2) The power formula assumes that the central-limit
     theorem is valid and hence is appropriate for large samples.

library(powerSurvEpi)

# Input parameters
nE <- 200           # Participants in experimental (treatment) group
nC <- 200           # Participants in control group
pE <- 0.3707        # Probability of event in experimental group
pC <- 0.4890        # Probability of event in control group
RR <- 0.7           # Hazard ratio (experimental vs. control)
alpha <- 0.05       # Significance level (two-sided)

# Call powerCT.default with Freedman approximation
power_value <- powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default(
  nE = nE,
  nC = nC,
  pE = pE,
  pC = pC,
  RR = RR,
  alpha = alpha
)

cat("Power Calculation using Freedman Approximation\n")
cat("==============================================\n")
cat("Method: powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default\n")
cat("Approximation: Freedman (1982)\n")
cat("Reference: Section 14.12 (page 807) of Rosner (2006)\n")
cat("Test: Two-sided log-rank test (Cox proportional-hazards model)\n")
cat("\n--- Input Parameters ---\n")
cat("Experimental group size (nE): ", nE, " participants\n")
cat("Control group size (nC): ", nC, " participants\n")
cat("Total sample size: ", nE + nC, " participants\n")
cat("Event probability in experimental group (pE): ", pE, "\n")
cat("Event probability in control group (pC): ", pC, "\n")
cat("Postulated hazard ratio (RR = HR_E/HR_C): ", RR, "\n")
cat("Significance level (alpha): ", alpha, "\n")
cat("Test direction: Two-sided\n")
cat("Allocation ratio: 1:1 (equal allocation)\n")
cat("Hypothesis: H0: RR = 1 vs. H1: RR ≠ 1\n")

cat("\n--- Derived Quantities (Freedman Approximation) ---\n")
m <- nE * pE + nC * pC
k <- nE / nC
z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)

cat("Total expected events (m = nE*pE + nC*pC): ", m, "\n")
cat("Allocation ratio (k = nE/nC): ", k, "\n")
cat("Critical z-value (z_1-α/2): ", z_crit, "\n")

# Validate the formula: power = Phi(sqrt(k*m) * |RR-1|/(k*RR+1) - z_1-α/2)
# where Phi is the standard normal CDF

numerator_part <- sqrt(k * m) * abs(RR - 1) / (k * RR + 1)
z_test <- numerator_part - z_crit
power_formula <- pnorm(z_test)

cat("\n--- Validation of Formula ---\n")
cat("Numerator part: sqrt(k*m) * |RR-1| / (k*RR+1) = ", numerator_part, "\n")
cat("z-test statistic: numerator - z_crit = ", z_test, "\n")
cat("Power (via formula): Phi(z_test) = ", power_formula, "\n")

cat("\n--- RESULT ---\n")
cat("Power computed by powerCT.default: ", power_value, "\n")
cat("Power via formula validation: ", power_formula, "\n")
cat("Match: ", isTRUE(all.equal(power_value, power_formula)), "\n")

# Output for structured reporting
POWER_AGENT_RESULT = list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "power",
      value = power_value,
      unit = "probability"
    )
  )
)

# Parameters
n_per_group <- 200
hr <- 0.7
p_treatment <- 0.3707
p_control <- 0.4890
alpha <- 0.05
two_sided <- TRUE

# The Freedman approximation requires hazard rates, not event probabilities directly.
# However, powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default expects parameters:
# - n: number of subjects per group
# - lambda0: event rate in control group
# - lambda1: event rate in treatment group (or HR relating to control)
# - alpha: significance level
# - power: if NULL, calculate power

# For the Freedman approximation with event probabilities, we need to interpret these
# as proportions of events. The hazard ratio of 0.7 means treatment has 0.7 times the
# hazard rate of control.

# Using powerSurvEpi::powerCT with specified parameters
result <- powerSurvEpi::powerCT(
  n = n_per_group,
  lambda0 = p_control,  # Event rate in control
  lambda1 = p_treatment,  # Event rate in treatment
  alpha = alpha,
  power = NULL,
  alternative = "two.sided"
)

# Extract power
power_value <- result$power

cat("Power Calculation using Freedman Approximation\n")
cat("==============================================\n")
cat("Method: powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default\n")
cat("Approximation: Freedman\n")
cat("Test: Two-sided log-rank\n")

cat("  Hazard ratio (HR): ", hr, "\n")
cat("  Significance level (alpha): ", alpha, "\n")
cat("  Test direction: Two-sided\n")
cat("  Allocation: 1:1\n")
cat("\nResult:\n")
cat("  Power: ", power_value, "\n")

POWER_AGENT_RESULT = list(

     Power calculation for the Comparison of Survival Curves Between
     Two Groups under the Cox Proportional-Hazards Model for clinical
     trials. Some parameters will be estimated based on a pilot data
     set.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     powerCT(formula, 
             dat, 
             nE, 
             nC, 
             RR, 
             alpha = 0.05)
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

 formula: A formula object, e.g. ‘Surv(time, status) ~ x’, where ‘time’
          is a vector of survival/censoring time, ‘status’ is a vector
          of censoring indicator, ‘x’ is the group indicator, which is
          a factor object in R and takes only two possible values (‘C’
          for control group and ‘E’ for experimental group). See also
          the documentation of the function ‘survfit’ in the library
          ‘survival’.

     dat: a data frame representing the pilot data set and containing
          at least 3 columns: (1) survival/censoring time; (2)
          censoring indicator; (3) group indicator which is a factor
          object in R and takes only two possible values (‘C’ for
          control group and ‘E’ for experimental group).

      nE: integer. number of participants in the experimental group.

      nC: integer. number of participants in the control group.

      RR: numeric. postulated hazard ratio.

   alpha: numeric. type I error rate.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     This is an implementation of the power calculation method
     described in Section 14.12 (page 807) of Rosner (2006). The method
     was proposed by Freedman (1982).

     The movitation of this function is that some times we do not have
     information about m or p_E and p_C available, but we have a pilot
     data set that can be used to estimate p_E and p_C hence m, where
     m=n_E p_E + n_C p_C is the expected total number of events over
     both groups, n_E and n_C are numbers of participants in group E
     (experimental group) and group C (control group), respectively.
     p_E is the probability of failure in group E (experimental group)
     over the maximum time period of the study (t years).  p_C is the
     probability of failure in group C (control group) over the maximum
     time period of the study (t years).

     Suppose we want to compare the survival curves between an
     experimental group (E) and a control group (C) in a clinical trial
     with a maximum follow-up of t years.  The Cox proportional hazards
     regression model is assumed to have the form:

                      h(t|X_1)=h_0(t)\exp(beta_1 X_1).                  
     
     Let n_E be the number of participants in the E group and n_C be
     the number of participants in the C group.  We wish to test the
     hypothesis H0: RR=1 versus H1: RR not equal to 1, where
     RR=\exp(beta_1)=underlying hazard ratio for the E group versus the
     C group. Let RR be the postulated hazard ratio, alpha be the
     significance level. Assume that the test is a two-sided test. If
     the ratio of participants in group E compared to group C =
     n_E/n_C=k, then the power of the test is

             power=Phi(sqrt{k*m}*|RR-1|/(k*RR+1)-z_{1-alpha/2}),        
     
     where

                             m=n_E p_E+n_C p_C,                         
     
     and z_{1-alpha/2} is the 100 (1-alpha/2)-th percentile of the
     standard normal distribution N(0, 1), Phi is the cumulative
     distribution function (CDF) of N(0, 1).

     p_C and p_E can be calculated from the following formulaes:

                 p_C=sum_{i=1}^{t}D_i, p_E=sum_{i=1}^{t}E_i,            
     
     where D_i=lambda_i A_i C_i, E_i=RRlambda_i B_i C_i,
     A_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-lambda_j),
     B_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-RRlambda_j),
     C_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-delta_j).  And lambda_i is the probability
     of failure at time ‘i’ among participants in the control group,
     given that a participant has survived to time i-1 and is not
     censored at time i-1, i.e., the approximate hazard time i in the
     control group, i=1,...,t; RRlambda_i is the probability of failure
     at time ‘i’ among participants in the experimental group, given
     that a participant has survived to time i-1 and is not censored at
     time i-1, i.e., the approximate hazard time i in the experimental
     group, i=1,...,t; delta is the prbability that a participant is
     censored at time i given that he was followed up to time i and has
     not failed, i=0, 1, ..., t, which is assumed the same in each
     group.

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

mat.lambda: a matrix with 9 columns and ‘nTimes+1’ rows, where ‘nTimes’
          is the number of observed time points for the control group
          in the data set. The 9 columns are (1) ‘time’ - observed time
          point for the control group; (2) ‘lambda’; (3) ‘RRlambda’;
          (4) ‘delta’; (5) ‘A’; (6) ‘B’; (7) ‘C’; (8) ‘D’; (9) ‘E’.
          Please refer to the Details section for the definitions of
          elements of these quantities. See also Table 14.24 on page
          809 of Rosner (2006).

mat.event: a matrix with 5 columns and ‘nTimes+1’ rows, where ‘nTimes’
          is the number of observed time points for control group in
          the data set. The 5 columns are (1) ‘time’ - observed time
          point for the control group; (2) ‘nEvent.C’ - number of
          events in the control group at each time point; (3)
          ‘nCensored.C’ - number of censorings in the control group at
          each time point; (4) ‘nSurvive.C’ - number of alived in the
          control group at each time point; (5) ‘nRisk.C’ - number of
          participants at risk in the control group at each time point.
          Please refer to Table 14.12 on page 787 of Rosner (2006).

      pC: estimated probability of failure in group C (control group)
          over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      pE: estimated probability of failure in group E (experimental
          group) over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

   power: the power of the test.

_ N_ o_ t_ e:

     (1) The estimates of RRlambda_i=RR*lambda_i. That is, ‘RRlambda’
     is not directly estimated based on data from the experimental
     group; (2) The power formula assumes that the central-limit
     theorem is valid and hence is appropriate for large samples.

_ R_ e_ f_ e_ r_ e_ n_ c_ e_ s:

     Freedman, L.S. (1982).  Tables of the number of patients required
     in clinical trials using the log-rank test.  _Statistics in
     Medicine_. 1: 121-129

     Rosner B. (2006).  _Fundamentals of Biostatistics_. (6-th
     edition). Thomson Brooks/Cole.

_ S_ e_ e _ A_ l_ s_ o:

     ‘powerCT.default0’, ‘powerCT.default’

_ E_ x_ a_ m_ p_ l_ e_ s:

       # Example 14.42 in Rosner B. Fundamentals of Biostatistics. 
       # (6-th edition). (2006) page 809
     
       library(survival)
     
       data(Oph)
       res <- powerCT(formula = Surv(times, status) ~ group, 
                      dat = Oph, 
                      nE = 200, 
                      nC = 200, 
                      RR = 0.7, 
                      alpha = 0.05)
     
       # Table 14.24 on page 809 of Rosner (2006)
       print(round(res$mat.lambda, 4))
     
       # Table 14.12 on page 787 of Rosner (2006)
       print(round(res$mat.event, 4))
     
       # the power
       print(round(res$power, 2))

plan.estimand: Difference in rates per child-week between treatment and control arms (0.005 vs 0.010)
plan.hypothesis: Two-sided test of equality of cluster-level event rates
assumptions: Cluster rates follow a model with additive one-cluster correction to the coefficient-of-variation formula
Between-cluster coefficient of variation is constant across treatment and control arms
Equal allocation (1:1 ratio) across arms
Two-sided significance level 0.05
Target power 90%
scientific_notes: The cluster-rate coefficient-of-variation method accounts for heterogeneity in cluster sizes and between-cluster variation in event rates
The additive one-cluster correction adjusts the design effect formula to improve accuracy for small cluster counts
Rates are specified per child-week, with total exposure per cluster fixed at 2500 child-weeks
This is a prospective power analysis for sample size calculation

answer.summary: For a two-arm cluster-randomized trial comparing event rates (treatment 0.005 vs. control 0.010 per child-week) with 2500 child-weeks exposure per cluster, between-cluster coefficient of variation 0.15, targeting 90% power at two-sided α = 0.05 with equal allocation, the cluster-rate coefficient-of-variation approximation including the additive one-cluster correction yields 145 clusters per arm (290 total clusters). Achieved power at this design is 0.9012; the preceding design (144 clusters per arm) achieves 0.8993 power.
answer.method: Cluster-rate coefficient-of-variation (CV) approximation with additive one-cluster correction. Variance per cluster rate modeled as [1/exposure + CV²] × λ, where exposure = 2500 child-weeks and CV = 0.15. Sample size per arm = ⌈[(z_α + z_β)² × (σ_t² + σ_c²)] / Δ² + 1⌉, where z_α = 1.960 (two-sided, α = 0.05), z_β = 1.282 (power = 0.90), Δ = 0.005 is the absolute difference in rates. Integer result obtained by standard rounding.
assumptions: Event counts within each cluster follow a Poisson distribution with rate λ per child-week
Between-cluster variation in true event rates is characterized by a constant coefficient of variation CV = 0.15 across both treatment and control arms
Exposure per cluster is fixed at exactly 2500 child-weeks
Equal cluster allocation (1:1 ratio) across treatment and control arms
Two-sided hypothesis test of rate difference with significance level α = 0.05
Additive one-cluster correction improves accuracy of sample size formula for discrete cluster counts
Treatment arm rate = 0.005 per child-week; control arm rate = 0.010 per child-week
limitations: The CV approximation assumes a particular variance structure (sampling + between-cluster heterogeneity) and may not fully capture complex or non-constant between-cluster variation
Assumes fixed exposure per cluster; actual variations in child-week accrual per cluster may affect realized power
Does not account for loss to follow-up, non-adherence, or other missing data mechanisms unless incorporated into the rates a priori
One-cluster additive correction is a heuristic adjustment; validity depends on large-sample approximation holding for the resulting design
No adjustment for multiple comparisons, interim analyses, or other multiplicity issues

executions.code:
# Cluster-rate coefficient-of-variation approximation with additive one-cluster correction
# for comparing two rates in cluster-randomized designs

# Study parameters
lambda_t <- 0.005       # treatment rate (events per child-week)
lambda_c <- 0.010       # control rate (events per child-week)
exposure <- 2500        # child-weeks per cluster
cv <- 0.15              # between-cluster coefficient of variation
alpha <- 0.05           # two-sided significance level
target_power <- 0.90    # target power
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)  # two-sided critical value

# Calculate expected events per cluster under each arm
mu_t <- lambda_t * exposure  # treatment: 0.005 * 2500 = 12.5
mu_c <- lambda_c * exposure  # control: 0.010 * 2500 = 25

cat("Expected events per cluster:\n")
cat("Treatment:", mu_t, "\n")
cat("Control:", mu_c, "\n\n")

# For cluster-rate data with CV specification, the variance is typically modeled as:
# Var(cluster count) = mu + (cv*mu)^2
# This accounts for both Poisson variation and between-cluster heterogeneity

# Under the cluster-rate CV approximation with additive one-cluster correction:
# The design effect approach accounts for clustering by adjusting the variance

# The variance of the cluster rate (per cluster) is:
# Var(rate_j) where rate_j ~ some distribution reflecting between-cluster variation
# A standard approach: if CV represents between-cluster variation in true rates,
# and we observe counts y_j ~ Poisson(exposure * lambda_j),
# then the variance of the observed cluster mean rate is:
# Var(y_j/exposure) = lambda/exposure + (cv*lambda)^2

# For the unpooled estimate of the mean difference:
# The variance of the difference in cluster means needs to account for the design effect

# Using the cluster-rate CV formula (Eldridge & Kerry, others):
# For a two-arm comparison, the number of clusters per arm is:
# k = [(z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (sigma_t^2 + sigma_c^2)] / (delta^2)
# where delta = lambda_t - lambda_c (signed difference)
# and sigma_j^2 includes both sampling and between-cluster variation

# The cluster-level variance under the CV model:
# Var(cluster count) = mu + (cv*mu)^2 (sampling + heterogeneity)
# Var(cluster rate) = [mu + (cv*mu)^2] / exposure^2

# For cluster-randomized trials with between-cluster variation in rates,
# one formulation uses:
# sigma_j^2 = [1/exposure + cv^2] * lambda_j

var_t_component <- (1/exposure + cv^2) * lambda_t
var_c_component <- (1/exposure + cv^2) * lambda_c

cat("Variance components (per-rate scale):\n")
cat("Treatment:", var_t_component, "\n")
cat("Control:", var_c_component, "\n")
cat("Sum:", var_t_component + var_c_component, "\n\n")

# Effect size
delta <- lambda_c - lambda_t  # Difference in rates (control minus treatment)
cat("Effect size (control - treatment):", delta, "\n\n")

# Beta for 90% power
z_beta <- qnorm(target_power)
cat("z_beta for 90% power:", z_beta, "\n")
cat("z_alpha (two-sided 0.05):", z_alpha, "\n\n")

# Basic sample size formula (without additive one-cluster correction):
k_basic <- ((z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_t_component + var_c_component)) / (delta^2)

cat("Clusters per arm (basic CV formula):", k_basic, "\n\n")

# Additive one-cluster correction: 
# This adjusts for the discrete nature of cluster counts and improves accuracy
# A simple additive correction adds 1 cluster to the design
k_corrected <- k_basic + 1

cat("Clusters per arm (with additive one-cluster correction):", k_corrected, "\n\n")

# Round to nearest integer for practical implementation
k_rounded <- round(k_corrected)

cat("Clusters per arm (rounded to integer):", k_rounded, "\n\n")

# Verification: compute actual power at the chosen design
k_final <- k_rounded
z_critical <- z_alpha  # two-sided critical value
se_diff <- sqrt((var_t_component + var_c_component) / k_final)
z_achieved <- delta / se_diff
achieved_power <- pnorm(z_achieved - z_alpha) + pnorm(-z_achieved - z_alpha)

cat("=== Verification at n =", k_final, "clusters per arm ===\n")
cat("Standard error of difference:", se_diff, "\n")
cat("Z-statistic under true effect:", z_achieved, "\n")
cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", achieved_power, "\n\n")

# Also check power at k_final - 1 (preceding admissible design)
k_prev <- k_final - 1
if (k_prev > 0) {
  se_diff_prev <- sqrt((var_t_component + var_c_component) / k_prev)
  z_achieved_prev <- delta / se_diff_prev
  achieved_power_prev <- pnorm(z_achieved_prev - z_alpha) + pnorm(-z_achieved_prev - z_alpha)
  
  cat("=== Verification at n =", k_prev, "clusters per arm ===\n")
  cat("Standard error of difference:", se_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("Z-statistic under true effect:", z_achieved_prev, "\n")
  cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", achieved_power_prev, "\n\n")
}

# Summary output
cat("\n=== FINAL RESULT ===\n")
cat("Sample size (integer clusters per arm):", k_final, "\n")
cat("Total clusters (both arms):", 2 * k_final, "\n")
cat("Achieved power:", round(achieved_power, 4), "\n")

# Emit structured result
results <- list(
  sample_size = k_final,
  total_clusters = 2 * k_final,
  achieved_power = round(achieved_power, 4),
  power_preceding_design = if(k_prev > 0) round(achieved_power_prev, 4) else NA,
  preceding_design_clusters_per_arm = k_prev
)

cat("\n")
print(results)

z_beta <- qnorm(target_power)

var_t_component <- (1/exposure + cv^2) * lambda_t
var_c_component <- (1/exposure + cv^2) * lambda_c

k_basic <- ((z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_t_component + var_c_component)) / (delta^2)

plan.estimand: Difference in rates per child-week between treatment and control arms (0.005 vs 0.010)
plan.hypothesis: Two-sided test of equality of cluster-level event rates
assumptions: Cluster rates follow a model with additive one-cluster correction to the coefficient-of-variation formula
Between-cluster coefficient of variation is constant across treatment and control arms
Equal allocation (1:1 ratio) across arms
Two-sided significance level 0.05
Target power 90%
scientific_notes: The cluster-rate coefficient-of-variation method accounts for heterogeneity in cluster sizes and between-cluster variation in event rates
The additive one-cluster correction adjusts the design effect formula to improve accuracy for small cluster counts
Rates are specified per child-week, with total exposure per cluster fixed at 2500 child-weeks
This is a prospective power analysis for sample size calculation

trace.code:
# Cluster-rate coefficient-of-variation approximation with additive one-cluster correction
# for comparing two rates in cluster-randomized designs

# Study parameters
lambda_t <- 0.005       # treatment rate (events per child-week)
lambda_c <- 0.010       # control rate (events per child-week)
exposure <- 2500        # child-weeks per cluster
cv <- 0.15              # between-cluster coefficient of variation
alpha <- 0.05           # two-sided significance level
target_power <- 0.90    # target power
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)  # two-sided critical value

# Calculate expected events per cluster under each arm
mu_t <- lambda_t * exposure  # treatment: 0.005 * 2500 = 12.5
mu_c <- lambda_c * exposure  # control: 0.010 * 2500 = 25

cat("Expected events per cluster:\n")
cat("Treatment:", mu_t, "\n")
cat("Control:", mu_c, "\n\n")

# For cluster-rate data with CV specification, the variance is typically modeled as:
# Var(cluster count) = mu + (cv*mu)^2
# This accounts for both Poisson variation and between-cluster heterogeneity

# Under the cluster-rate CV approximation with additive one-cluster correction:
# The design effect approach accounts for clustering by adjusting the variance

# The variance of the cluster rate (per cluster) is:
# Var(rate_j) where rate_j ~ some distribution reflecting between-cluster variation
# A standard approach: if CV represents between-cluster variation in true rates,
# and we observe counts y_j ~ Poisson(exposure * lambda_j),
# then the variance of the observed cluster mean rate is:
# Var(y_j/exposure) = lambda/exposure + (cv*lambda)^2

# For the unpooled estimate of the mean difference:
# The variance of the difference in cluster means needs to account for the design effect

# Using the cluster-rate CV formula (Eldridge & Kerry, others):
# For a two-arm comparison, the number of clusters per arm is:
# k = [(z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (sigma_t^2 + sigma_c^2)] / (delta^2)
# where delta = lambda_t - lambda_c (signed difference)
# and sigma_j^2 includes both sampling and between-cluster variation

# The cluster-level variance under the CV model:
# Var(cluster count) = mu + (cv*mu)^2 (sampling + heterogeneity)
# Var(cluster rate) = [mu + (cv*mu)^2] / exposure^2

# For cluster-randomized trials with between-cluster variation in rates,
# one formulation uses:
# sigma_j^2 = [1/exposure + cv^2] * lambda_j

var_t_component <- (1/exposure + cv^2) * lambda_t
var_c_component <- (1/exposure + cv^2) * lambda_c

cat("Variance components (per-rate scale):\n")
cat("Treatment:", var_t_component, "\n")
cat("Control:", var_c_component, "\n")
cat("Sum:", var_t_component + var_c_component, "\n\n")

# Effect size
delta <- lambda_c - lambda_t  # Difference in rates (control minus treatment)
cat("Effect size (control - treatment):", delta, "\n\n")

# Beta for 90% power
z_beta <- qnorm(target_power)
cat("z_beta for 90% power:", z_beta, "\n")
cat("z_alpha (two-sided 0.05):", z_alpha, "\n\n")

# Basic sample size formula (without additive one-cluster correction):
k_basic <- ((z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_t_component + var_c_component)) / (delta^2)

cat("Clusters per arm (basic CV formula):", k_basic, "\n\n")

# Additive one-cluster correction: 
# This adjusts for the discrete nature of cluster counts and improves accuracy
# A simple additive correction adds 1 cluster to the design
k_corrected <- k_basic + 1

cat("Clusters per arm (with additive one-cluster correction):", k_corrected, "\n\n")

# Round to nearest integer for practical implementation
k_rounded <- round(k_corrected)

cat("Clusters per arm (rounded to integer):", k_rounded, "\n\n")

# Verification: compute actual power at the chosen design
k_final <- k_rounded
z_critical <- z_alpha  # two-sided critical value
se_diff <- sqrt((var_t_component + var_c_component) / k_final)
z_achieved <- delta / se_diff
achieved_power <- pnorm(z_achieved - z_alpha) + pnorm(-z_achieved - z_alpha)

cat("=== Verification at n =", k_final, "clusters per arm ===\n")
cat("Standard error of difference:", se_diff, "\n")
cat("Z-statistic under true effect:", z_achieved, "\n")
cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", achieved_power, "\n\n")

# Also check power at k_final - 1 (preceding admissible design)
k_prev <- k_final - 1
if (k_prev > 0) {
  se_diff_prev <- sqrt((var_t_component + var_c_component) / k_prev)
  z_achieved_prev <- delta / se_diff_prev
  achieved_power_prev <- pnorm(z_achieved_prev - z_alpha) + pnorm(-z_achieved_prev - z_alpha)
  
  cat("=== Verification at n =", k_prev, "clusters per arm ===\n")
  cat("Standard error of difference:", se_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("Z-statistic under true effect:", z_achieved_prev, "\n")
  cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", achieved_power_prev, "\n\n")
}

# Summary output
cat("\n=== FINAL RESULT ===\n")
cat("Sample size (integer clusters per arm):", k_final, "\n")
cat("Total clusters (both arms):", 2 * k_final, "\n")
cat("Achieved power:", round(achieved_power, 4), "\n")

# Emit structured result
results <- list(
  sample_size = k_final,
  total_clusters = 2 * k_final,
  achieved_power = round(achieved_power, 4),
  power_preceding_design = if(k_prev > 0) round(achieved_power_prev, 4) else NA,
  preceding_design_clusters_per_arm = k_prev
)

cat("\n")
print(results)

# Evidence e1; success=true

# Cluster-rate coefficient-of-variation approximation with additive one-cluster correction
# for comparing two rates in cluster-randomized designs

# Study parameters
lambda_t <- 0.005       # treatment rate (events per child-week)
lambda_c <- 0.010       # control rate (events per child-week)
exposure <- 2500        # child-weeks per cluster
cv <- 0.15              # between-cluster coefficient of variation
alpha <- 0.05           # two-sided significance level
target_power <- 0.90    # target power
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)  # two-sided critical value

# Calculate expected events per cluster under each arm
mu_t <- lambda_t * exposure  # treatment: 0.005 * 2500 = 12.5
mu_c <- lambda_c * exposure  # control: 0.010 * 2500 = 25

cat("Expected events per cluster:\n")
cat("Treatment:", mu_t, "\n")
cat("Control:", mu_c, "\n\n")

# For cluster-rate data with CV specification, the variance is typically modeled as:
# Var(cluster count) = mu + (cv*mu)^2
# This accounts for both Poisson variation and between-cluster heterogeneity

# Under the cluster-rate CV approximation with additive one-cluster correction:
# The design effect approach accounts for clustering by adjusting the variance

# The variance of the cluster rate (per cluster) is:
# Var(rate_j) where rate_j ~ some distribution reflecting between-cluster variation
# A standard approach: if CV represents between-cluster variation in true rates,
# and we observe counts y_j ~ Poisson(exposure * lambda_j),
# then the variance of the observed cluster mean rate is:
# Var(y_j/exposure) = lambda/exposure + (cv*lambda)^2

# For the unpooled estimate of the mean difference:
# The variance of the difference in cluster means needs to account for the design effect

# Using the cluster-rate CV formula (Eldridge & Kerry, others):
# For a two-arm comparison, the number of clusters per arm is:
# k = [(z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (sigma_t^2 + sigma_c^2)] / (delta^2)
# where delta = lambda_t - lambda_c (signed difference)
# and sigma_j^2 includes both sampling and between-cluster variation

# The cluster-level variance under the CV model:
# Var(cluster count) = mu + (cv*mu)^2 (sampling + heterogeneity)
# Var(cluster rate) = [mu + (cv*mu)^2] / exposure^2

# For cluster-randomized trials with between-cluster variation in rates,
# one formulation uses:
# sigma_j^2 = [1/exposure + cv^2] * lambda_j

var_t_component <- (1/exposure + cv^2) * lambda_t
var_c_component <- (1/exposure + cv^2) * lambda_c

cat("Variance components (per-rate scale):\n")
cat("Treatment:", var_t_component, "\n")
cat("Control:", var_c_component, "\n")
cat("Sum:", var_t_component + var_c_component, "\n\n")

# Effect size
delta <- lambda_c - lambda_t  # Difference in rates (control minus treatment)
cat("Effect size (control - treatment):", delta, "\n\n")

# Beta for 90% power
z_beta <- qnorm(target_power)
cat("z_beta for 90% power:", z_beta, "\n")
cat("z_alpha (two-sided 0.05):", z_alpha, "\n\n")

# Basic sample size formula (without additive one-cluster correction):
k_basic <- ((z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_t_component + var_c_component)) / (delta^2)

cat("Clusters per arm (basic CV formula):", k_basic, "\n\n")

# Additive one-cluster correction: 
# This adjusts for the discrete nature of cluster counts and improves accuracy
# A simple additive correction adds 1 cluster to the design
k_corrected <- k_basic + 1

cat("Clusters per arm (with additive one-cluster correction):", k_corrected, "\n\n")

# Round to nearest integer for practical implementation
k_rounded <- round(k_corrected)

cat("Clusters per arm (rounded to integer):", k_rounded, "\n\n")

# Verification: compute actual power at the chosen design
k_final <- k_rounded
z_critical <- z_alpha  # two-sided critical value
se_diff <- sqrt((var_t_component + var_c_component) / k_final)
z_achieved <- delta / se_diff
achieved_power <- pnorm(z_achieved - z_alpha) + pnorm(-z_achieved - z_alpha)

cat("=== Verification at n =", k_final, "clusters per arm ===\n")
cat("Standard error of difference:", se_diff, "\n")
cat("Z-statistic under true effect:", z_achieved, "\n")
cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", achieved_power, "\n\n")

# Also check power at k_final - 1 (preceding admissible design)
k_prev <- k_final - 1
if (k_prev > 0) {
  se_diff_prev <- sqrt((var_t_component + var_c_component) / k_prev)
  z_achieved_prev <- delta / se_diff_prev
  achieved_power_prev <- pnorm(z_achieved_prev - z_alpha) + pnorm(-z_achieved_prev - z_alpha)
  
  cat("=== Verification at n =", k_prev, "clusters per arm ===\n")
  cat("Standard error of difference:", se_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("Z-statistic under true effect:", z_achieved_prev, "\n")
  cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", achieved_power_prev, "\n\n")
}

# Summary output
cat("\n=== FINAL RESULT ===\n")
cat("Sample size (integer clusters per arm):", k_final, "\n")
cat("Total clusters (both arms):", 2 * k_final, "\n")
cat("Achieved power:", round(achieved_power, 4), "\n")

# Emit structured result
results <- list(
  sample_size = k_final,
  total_clusters = 2 * k_final,
  achieved_power = round(achieved_power, 4),
  power_preceding_design = if(k_prev > 0) round(achieved_power_prev, 4) else NA,
  preceding_design_clusters_per_arm = k_prev
)

cat("\n")
print(results)

answer.summary: Sample size calculation for a two-armed cluster-randomized trial comparing incidence rates (treatment 0.005 vs control 0.010 per child-week) using the coefficient-of-variation approximation from Hayes & Moulton Field Trials of Health Interventions Chapter 5, Section 6.1, with additive one-cluster continuity correction. Target: 90% power, two-sided α=0.05, equal allocation. Result: 52,559 clusters per arm (105,118 total), achieving 0.900009 power.
answer.method: Cluster-rate coefficient-of-variation approximation (Hayes & Moulton, Field Trials Chapter 5, Section 6.1). Variance per cluster computed as Var(rate) = [1 + k·μ·CV²]/(k·μ), where k = 2500 child-weeks per cluster, μ = expected event count (μ_t = 12.5 for treatment, μ_c = 25 for control), CV = 0.25 (between-cluster coefficient of variation). For equal allocation, sample size formula: m = (Z_{α/2} + Z_β)² × (Var_t + Var_c) / (δ)², where Z_{α/2} = 1.959964 (two-sided α=0.05), Z_β = 1.281552 (power=0.90), and δ = 0.005. Continuous solution m = 52,557.29. Additive one-cluster correction yields m = 52,558.29. Rounded upward to m = 52,559. Power verified using two-sided normal approximation: standardized effect z_effect = 3.241568; achieved power = 0.900009.
assumptions: Incidence counts at the individual level follow a Poisson distribution
Between-cluster heterogeneity in rates is characterized by a gamma mixture with coefficient of variation 0.25
Exposure is fixed at 2500 child-weeks per cluster, constant across all clusters
Treatment and control arms have equal allocation (1:1)
Two-sided Wald-type normal-approximation Z-test with significance level 0.05
Additive one-cluster continuity correction applied per Hayes & Moulton finite-sample adjustment
limitations: Sample size is very large (>52,000 clusters per arm), suggesting operational infeasibility for many real-world settings
The CV approximation is parsimonious but represents between-cluster variation via a single parameter
Normal approximation validity depends on adequate expected event counts; exact or simulation-based methods would provide additional verification
Assumes constant exposure (child-weeks) per cluster; variable exposure would require adjustment

# Cluster-rate coefficient-of-variation approximation
# Field Trials of Health Interventions, Chapter 5, Section 6.1
# with additive one-cluster correction

# Parameters
treatment_rate <- 0.005  # per child-week
control_rate <- 0.010    # per child-week
exposure_per_cluster <- 2500  # child-weeks
between_cluster_cv <- 0.25    # dimensionless
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.90
allocation_ratio <- 1  # equal allocation

# Expected number of events per cluster (mean)
mu_t <- treatment_rate * exposure_per_cluster
mu_c <- control_rate * exposure_per_cluster

cat("Treatment rate (per child-week):", treatment_rate, "\n")
cat("Control rate (per child-week):", control_rate, "\n")
cat("Exposure per cluster (child-weeks):", exposure_per_cluster, "\n")
cat("Between-cluster CV:", between_cluster_cv, "\n")
cat("Expected events per cluster (treatment):", mu_t, "\n")
cat("Expected events per cluster (control):", mu_c, "\n\n")

# Two-sided critical value
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
z_beta <- qnorm(target_power)

cat("Two-sided alpha:", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("Z-value for alpha/2 (1 - 0.025):", z_alpha, "\n")
cat("Z-value for power (", target_power, "):", z_beta, "\n\n")

# CV approximation formula for cluster-level rates
# The variance for cluster-level rate differences includes:
# 1. Poisson variation at individual level
# 2. Between-cluster variation captured via CV

# For equal allocation, the variance of rate difference is:
# Var(r_t - r_c) = Var(r_t) + Var(r_c)
# where Var(r) includes both Poisson and between-cluster components

# Under the CV approximation:
# Var(r_t) ≈ [mu_t + (mu_t * CV)^2] / exposure_per_cluster
# Var(r_c) ≈ [mu_c + (mu_c * CV)^2] / exposure_per_cluster

# For cluster-level aggregated data with Poisson base and gamma mixing:
# Variance includes: mu/exposure + (mu*CV)^2/exposure
# But the formula accounts for the between-cluster variance directly

# Using Hayes & Moulton formula for cluster-rate studies
# The effective variance for one cluster in each arm is:
# V_t = (1/mu_t + CV^2) / exposure_per_cluster  (approx. for treatment)
# V_c = (1/mu_c + CV^2) / exposure_per_cluster  (approx. for control)

# More precisely, for counts Y ~ negative binomial (Poisson-gamma mixture):
# Var(Y) = mu + (mu * CV)^2
# For rates, Var(rate) = Var(count) / exposure^2

# Hayes & Moulton Section 6.1 uses:
# Var of cluster rate = (1 + k*mu*CV^2) / (k*mu)
# where k is the number of observations per cluster (here: exposure_per_cluster)

k <- exposure_per_cluster

# Variance for treatment arm (per cluster)
var_rate_t <- (1 + k * mu_t * (between_cluster_cv^2)) / (k * mu_t)

# Variance for control arm (per cluster)
var_rate_c <- (1 + k * mu_c * (between_cluster_cv^2)) / (k * mu_c)

cat("Variance of cluster rate (treatment):", var_rate_t, "\n")
cat("Variance of cluster rate (control):", var_rate_c, "\n\n")

# Rate difference
rate_diff <- treatment_rate - control_rate
cat("Rate difference (treatment - control):", rate_diff, "\n\n")

# For equal allocation with m clusters per arm:
# Var(rate_diff) = var_rate_t/m + var_rate_c/m = (var_rate_t + var_rate_c)/m

# Sample size formula: m = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / (rate_diff)^2

m_continuous <- ((z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_rate_t + var_rate_c)) / (rate_diff^2)

cat("Continuous sample size (clusters per arm, before correction):", m_continuous, "\n\n")

# Additive one-cluster correction (Hayes & Moulton)
# This is a finite-sample continuity adjustment
m_with_correction <- m_continuous + 1

cat("Sample size with one-cluster additive correction:", m_with_correction, "\n\n")

# Round upward to ensure power meets or exceeds target
m_rounded <- ceiling(m_with_correction)

cat("Sample size rounded upward (clusters per arm):", m_rounded, "\n")
cat("Total clusters:", m_rounded * 2, "\n\n")

# Verify achieved power at rounded design
# For verification, calculate power at m_rounded
m_check <- m_rounded

# Variance of rate difference with m_check clusters per arm
var_diff_check <- (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / m_check

# Standard error
se_diff_check <- sqrt(var_diff_check)

# Non-centrality parameter
ncp_check <- rate_diff / se_diff_check

# Achieved power (two-sided)
achieved_power <- 2 * pnorm(ncp_check - z_alpha) - 1

cat("Verification at m =", m_rounded, ":\n")
cat("Variance of rate difference:", var_diff_check, "\n")
cat("Standard error of rate difference:", se_diff_check, "\n")
cat("Non-centrality parameter:", ncp_check, "\n")
cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", round(achieved_power, 6), "\n\n")

# Also verify power at m_rounded - 1 to show rounding impact
if (m_rounded > 1) {
  m_prev <- m_rounded - 1
  var_diff_prev <- (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / m_prev
  se_diff_prev <- sqrt(var_diff_prev)
  ncp_prev <- rate_diff / se_diff_prev
  achieved_power_prev <- 2 * pnorm(ncp_prev - z_alpha) - 1
  
  cat("Verification at m =", m_prev, "(preceding admissible design):\n")
  cat("Variance of rate difference:", var_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("Standard error of rate difference:", se_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("Non-centrality parameter:", ncp_prev, "\n")
  cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", round(achieved_power_prev, 6), "\n\n")
}

# Final result
POWER_AGENT_RESULT=jsonlite::toJSON(list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = m_rounded, unit = "clusters_per_arm"),
    list(metric = "achieved_power", value = round(achieved_power, 6), unit = "proportion")
  ),
  study_design = list(
    method = "cluster_rate_cv",
    treatment_rate = treatment_rate,
    control_rate = control_rate,
    exposure_per_cluster = exposure_per_cluster,
    between_cluster_cv = between_cluster_cv,
    alpha = alpha,
    target_power = target_power,
    sidedness = "two-sided",
    allocation_ratio = 1
  )
), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15)

# Field Trials of Health Interventions, Chapter 5, Section 6.1
# with additive one-cluster correction

# Parameters
treatment_rate <- 0.005  # per child-week
control_rate <- 0.010    # per child-week
exposure_per_cluster <- 2500  # child-weeks
between_cluster_cv <- 0.25    # dimensionless
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.90
allocation_ratio <- 1  # equal allocation

# Expected number of events per cluster (mean)
mu_t <- treatment_rate * exposure_per_cluster
mu_c <- control_rate * exposure_per_cluster

cat("Treatment rate (per child-week):", treatment_rate, "\n")
cat("Control rate (per child-week):", control_rate, "\n")
cat("Exposure per cluster (child-weeks):", exposure_per_cluster, "\n")
cat("Between-cluster CV:", between_cluster_cv, "\n")
cat("Expected events per cluster (treatment):", mu_t, "\n")
cat("Expected events per cluster (control):", mu_c, "\n\n")

# Two-sided critical value
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
z_beta <- qnorm(target_power)

cat("Two-sided alpha:", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("Z-value for alpha/2 (1 - 0.025):", z_alpha, "\n")
cat("Z-value for power (", target_power, "):", z_beta, "\n\n")

# Using Hayes & Moulton formula for cluster-rate studies
# Var of cluster rate = (1 + k*mu*CV^2) / (k*mu)
# where k is the number of observations per cluster (here: exposure_per_cluster)

k <- exposure_per_cluster

# Variance for treatment arm (per cluster)
var_rate_t <- (1 + k * mu_t * (between_cluster_cv^2)) / (k * mu_t)

# Variance for control arm (per cluster)
var_rate_c <- (1 + k * mu_c * (between_cluster_cv^2)) / (k * mu_c)

cat("Variance of cluster rate (treatment):", var_rate_t, "\n")
cat("Variance of cluster rate (control):", var_rate_c, "\n\n")

# Absolute rate difference
rate_diff <- abs(treatment_rate - control_rate)
cat("Absolute rate difference |treatment - control|:", rate_diff, "\n\n")

# Sample size formula: m = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / (rate_diff)^2

m_continuous <- ((z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_rate_t + var_rate_c)) / (rate_diff^2)

cat("Continuous sample size (clusters per arm, before correction):", m_continuous, "\n\n")

# Additive one-cluster correction (Hayes & Moulton)
# This is a finite-sample continuity adjustment
m_with_correction <- m_continuous + 1

cat("Sample size with one-cluster additive correction:", m_with_correction, "\n\n")

# Round upward to ensure power meets or exceeds target
m_rounded <- ceiling(m_with_correction)

cat("Sample size rounded upward (clusters per arm):", m_rounded, "\n")
cat("Total clusters:", m_rounded * 2, "\n\n")

# Verify achieved power at rounded design
# For a two-sided test of H0: rate_diff = 0 vs H1: rate_diff ≠ 0
# Under H0, the test statistic Z ~ N(0, 1)
# Under H1, the test statistic is approximately N(effect / SE, 1)
# where effect = true difference = rate_diff, SE = sqrt(var(rate_diff))

m_check <- m_rounded

# Variance of rate difference with m_check clusters per arm
var_diff_check <- (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / m_check

# Standard error
se_diff_check <- sqrt(var_diff_check)

# Standardized effect (non-centrality in units of SE)
z_effect <- rate_diff / se_diff_check

# For a two-sided test at significance level alpha:
# We reject if |Z_observed| > z_alpha/2
# Under H1, Z_observed ~ N(z_effect, 1)
# Power = P(|Z| > z_alpha/2 | H1)
#       = P(Z > z_alpha/2) + P(Z < -z_alpha/2) under N(z_effect, 1)
#       = P(Z - z_effect > z_alpha/2 - z_effect) + P(Z - z_effect < -z_alpha/2 - z_effect)
#       = Phi(z_effect - z_alpha/2) + Phi(-z_effect - z_alpha/2)
# where Phi is the standard normal CDF

achieved_power <- pnorm(z_effect - z_alpha) + pnorm(-z_effect - z_alpha)

cat("Verification at m =", m_rounded, ":\n")
cat("Variance of rate difference:", var_diff_check, "\n")
cat("Standard error of rate difference:", se_diff_check, "\n")
cat("Standardized effect size (z_effect):", z_effect, "\n")
cat("z_alpha (two-sided, alpha/2):", z_alpha, "\n")
cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", round(achieved_power, 6), "\n\n")

# Also verify power at m_rounded - 1 to show rounding impact
if (m_rounded > 1) {
  m_prev <- m_rounded - 1
  var_diff_prev <- (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / m_prev
  se_diff_prev <- sqrt(var_diff_prev)
  z_effect_prev <- rate_diff / se_diff_prev
  achieved_power_prev <- pnorm(z_effect_prev - z_alpha) + pnorm(-z_effect_prev - z_alpha)
  
  cat("Verification at m =", m_prev, "(preceding admissible design):\n")
  cat("Variance of rate difference:", var_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("Standard error of rate difference:", se_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("Standardized effect size (z_effect):", z_effect_prev, "\n")
  cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", round(achieved_power_prev, 6), "\n\n")
}

# Final result
cat("\n=== FINAL RESULT ===\n")
cat("Clusters per arm (rounded upward):", m_rounded, "\n")
cat("Achieved power at selected design:", round(achieved_power, 6), "\n")

var_rate_c <- (1 + k * mu_c * (between_cluster_cv^2)) / (k * mu_c)

plan.hypothesis: Two-sided test of equality of cluster-level incidence rates
assumptions: Incidence rates follow Poisson distribution at individual level
Between-cluster heterogeneity in rates follows gamma distribution with coefficient of variation 0.25
Exposure is fixed at 2500 child-weeks per cluster
Additive one-cluster correction applied as specified in Field Trials text
Equal allocation between treatment and control arms
Two-sided Wald-type test with significance level 0.05
scientific_notes: Uses coefficient-of-variation approximation from Hayes & Moulton Field Trials of Health Interventions Chapter 5, Section 6.1
The CV approximation accounts for between-cluster heterogeneity in a more parsimonious way than full variance parameters
One-cluster additive correction is a finite-sample continuity adjustment recommended for small cluster counts

# Cluster-rate coefficient-of-variation approximation
# Field Trials of Health Interventions, Chapter 5, Section 6.1
# with additive one-cluster correction

# Parameters
treatment_rate <- 0.005  # per child-week
control_rate <- 0.010    # per child-week
exposure_per_cluster <- 2500  # child-weeks
between_cluster_cv <- 0.25    # dimensionless
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.90
allocation_ratio <- 1  # equal allocation

# Expected number of events per cluster (mean)
mu_t <- treatment_rate * exposure_per_cluster
mu_c <- control_rate * exposure_per_cluster

cat("Treatment rate (per child-week):", treatment_rate, "\n")
cat("Control rate (per child-week):", control_rate, "\n")
cat("Exposure per cluster (child-weeks):", exposure_per_cluster, "\n")
cat("Between-cluster CV:", between_cluster_cv, "\n")
cat("Expected events per cluster (treatment):", mu_t, "\n")
cat("Expected events per cluster (control):", mu_c, "\n\n")

# Two-sided critical value
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
z_beta <- qnorm(target_power)

cat("Two-sided alpha:", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("Z-value for alpha/2 (1 - 0.025):", z_alpha, "\n")
cat("Z-value for power (", target_power, "):", z_beta, "\n\n")

# CV approximation formula for cluster-level rates
# The variance for cluster-level rate differences includes:
# 1. Poisson variation at individual level
# 2. Between-cluster variation captured via CV

# For equal allocation, the variance of rate difference is:
# Var(r_t - r_c) = Var(r_t) + Var(r_c)
# where Var(r) includes both Poisson and between-cluster components

# Under the CV approximation:
# Var(r_t) ≈ [mu_t + (mu_t * CV)^2] / exposure_per_cluster
# Var(r_c) ≈ [mu_c + (mu_c * CV)^2] / exposure_per_cluster

# For cluster-level aggregated data with Poisson base and gamma mixing:
# Variance includes: mu/exposure + (mu*CV)^2/exposure
# But the formula accounts for the between-cluster variance directly

# Using Hayes & Moulton formula for cluster-rate studies
# The effective variance for one cluster in each arm is:
# V_t = (1/mu_t + CV^2) / exposure_per_cluster  (approx. for treatment)
# V_c = (1/mu_c + CV^2) / exposure_per_cluster  (approx. for control)

# More precisely, for counts Y ~ negative binomial (Poisson-gamma mixture):
# Var(Y) = mu + (mu * CV)^2
# For rates, Var(rate) = Var(count) / exposure^2

# Hayes & Moulton Section 6.1 uses:
# Var of cluster rate = (1 + k*mu*CV^2) / (k*mu)
# where k is the number of observations per cluster (here: exposure_per_cluster)

k <- exposure_per_cluster

# Variance for treatment arm (per cluster)
var_rate_t <- (1 + k * mu_t * (between_cluster_cv^2)) / (k * mu_t)

# Variance for control arm (per cluster)
var_rate_c <- (1 + k * mu_c * (between_cluster_cv^2)) / (k * mu_c)

cat("Variance of cluster rate (treatment):", var_rate_t, "\n")
cat("Variance of cluster rate (control):", var_rate_c, "\n\n")

# Rate difference
rate_diff <- treatment_rate - control_rate
cat("Rate difference (treatment - control):", rate_diff, "\n\n")

# For equal allocation with m clusters per arm:
# Var(rate_diff) = var_rate_t/m + var_rate_c/m = (var_rate_t + var_rate_c)/m

# Sample size formula: m = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / (rate_diff)^2

m_continuous <- ((z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_rate_t + var_rate_c)) / (rate_diff^2)

cat("Continuous sample size (clusters per arm, before correction):", m_continuous, "\n\n")

# Additive one-cluster correction (Hayes & Moulton)
# This is a finite-sample continuity adjustment
m_with_correction <- m_continuous + 1

cat("Sample size with one-cluster additive correction:", m_with_correction, "\n\n")

# Round upward to ensure power meets or exceeds target
m_rounded <- ceiling(m_with_correction)

cat("Sample size rounded upward (clusters per arm):", m_rounded, "\n")
cat("Total clusters:", m_rounded * 2, "\n\n")

# Verify achieved power at rounded design
# For verification, calculate power at m_rounded
m_check <- m_rounded

# Variance of rate difference with m_check clusters per arm
var_diff_check <- (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / m_check

# Standard error
se_diff_check <- sqrt(var_diff_check)

# Non-centrality parameter
ncp_check <- rate_diff / se_diff_check

# Achieved power (two-sided)
achieved_power <- 2 * pnorm(ncp_check - z_alpha) - 1

cat("Verification at m =", m_rounded, ":\n")
cat("Variance of rate difference:", var_diff_check, "\n")
cat("Standard error of rate difference:", se_diff_check, "\n")
cat("Non-centrality parameter:", ncp_check, "\n")
cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", round(achieved_power, 6), "\n\n")

# Also verify power at m_rounded - 1 to show rounding impact
if (m_rounded > 1) {
  m_prev <- m_rounded - 1
  var_diff_prev <- (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / m_prev
  se_diff_prev <- sqrt(var_diff_prev)
  ncp_prev <- rate_diff / se_diff_prev
  achieved_power_prev <- 2 * pnorm(ncp_prev - z_alpha) - 1
  
  cat("Verification at m =", m_prev, "(preceding admissible design):\n")
  cat("Variance of rate difference:", var_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("Standard error of rate difference:", se_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("Non-centrality parameter:", ncp_prev, "\n")
  cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", round(achieved_power_prev, 6), "\n\n")
}

# Final result
POWER_AGENT_RESULT=jsonlite::toJSON(list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = m_rounded, unit = "clusters_per_arm"),
    list(metric = "achieved_power", value = round(achieved_power, 6), unit = "proportion")
  ),
  study_design = list(
    method = "cluster_rate_cv",
    treatment_rate = treatment_rate,
    control_rate = control_rate,
    exposure_per_cluster = exposure_per_cluster,
    between_cluster_cv = between_cluster_cv,
    alpha = alpha,
    target_power = target_power,
    sidedness = "two-sided",
    allocation_ratio = 1
  )
), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15)

exposure_per_cluster <- 2500  # child-weeks
between_cluster_cv <- 0.25    # dimensionless

target_power <- 0.90
allocation_ratio <- 1  # equal allocation

# Expected number of events per cluster (mean)
mu_t <- treatment_rate * exposure_per_cluster
mu_c <- control_rate * exposure_per_cluster

cat("Treatment rate (per child-week):", treatment_rate, "\n")
cat("Control rate (per child-week):", control_rate, "\n")
cat("Exposure per cluster (child-weeks):", exposure_per_cluster, "\n")
cat("Between-cluster CV:", between_cluster_cv, "\n")
cat("Expected events per cluster (treatment):", mu_t, "\n")
cat("Expected events per cluster (control):", mu_c, "\n\n")

# Two-sided critical value
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
z_beta <- qnorm(target_power)

cat("Two-sided alpha:", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("Z-value for alpha/2 (1 - 0.025):", z_alpha, "\n")
cat("Z-value for power (", target_power, "):", z_beta, "\n\n")

# Using Hayes & Moulton formula for cluster-rate studies
# Var of cluster rate = (1 + k*mu*CV^2) / (k*mu)
# where k is the number of observations per cluster (here: exposure_per_cluster)

k <- exposure_per_cluster

# Variance for treatment arm (per cluster)
var_rate_t <- (1 + k * mu_t * (between_cluster_cv^2)) / (k * mu_t)

# Variance for control arm (per cluster)
var_rate_c <- (1 + k * mu_c * (between_cluster_cv^2)) / (k * mu_c)

cat("Variance of cluster rate (treatment):", var_rate_t, "\n")
cat("Variance of cluster rate (control):", var_rate_c, "\n\n")

# Absolute rate difference
rate_diff <- abs(treatment_rate - control_rate)
cat("Absolute rate difference |treatment - control|:", rate_diff, "\n\n")

# Sample size formula: m = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / (rate_diff)^2

m_continuous <- ((z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_rate_t + var_rate_c)) / (rate_diff^2)

cat("Continuous sample size (clusters per arm, before correction):", m_continuous, "\n\n")

# Additive one-cluster correction (Hayes & Moulton)
# This is a finite-sample continuity adjustment
m_with_correction <- m_continuous + 1

cat("Sample size with one-cluster additive correction:", m_with_correction, "\n\n")

m_rounded <- ceiling(m_with_correction)

cat("Sample size rounded upward (clusters per arm):", m_rounded, "\n")
cat("Total clusters:", m_rounded * 2, "\n\n")

# For a two-sided test of H0: rate_diff = 0 vs H1: rate_diff ≠ 0
# Under H0, the test statistic Z ~ N(0, 1)
# Under H1, the test statistic is approximately N(effect / SE, 1)

var_diff_check <- (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / m_check

achieved_power <- pnorm(z_effect - z_alpha) + pnorm(-z_effect - z_alpha)

cat("Verification at m =", m_rounded, ":\n")
cat("Variance of rate difference:", var_diff_check, "\n")
cat("Standard error of rate difference:", se_diff_check, "\n")
cat("Standardized effect size (z_effect):", z_effect, "\n")

  cat("Variance of rate difference:", var_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("Standard error of rate difference:", se_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("Standardized effect size (z_effect):", z_effect_prev, "\n")
  cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", round(achieved_power_prev, 6), "\n\n")

# Cluster-rate coefficient-of-variation approximation
# Field Trials of Health Interventions, Chapter 5, Section 6.1

cat("=" %*% rep("=", 80), "\n")
cat("SAMPLE SIZE CALCULATION: CLUSTER-RATE INCIDENCE STUDY\n")
cat("=" %*% rep("=", 80), "\n\n")

# Input parameters
treatment_rate <- 0.005
control_rate <- 0.010
exposure_per_cluster <- 2500
between_cluster_cv <- 0.25
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.90

# Computed parameters
mu_t <- treatment_rate * exposure_per_cluster  # 12.5 events
mu_c <- control_rate * exposure_per_cluster    # 25 events
k <- exposure_per_cluster
rate_diff <- abs(treatment_rate - control_rate)
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
z_beta <- qnorm(target_power)

# Variance components
var_rate_t <- (1 + k * mu_t * (between_cluster_cv^2)) / (k * mu_t)
var_rate_c <- (1 + k * mu_c * (between_cluster_cv^2)) / (k * mu_c)

cat("STUDY DESIGN PARAMETERS\n")
cat("-" %*% rep("-", 80), "\n")
cat("Treatment incidence rate:             ", treatment_rate, "per child-week\n")
cat("Control incidence rate:                ", control_rate, "per child-week\n")
cat("Exposure per cluster:                  ", exposure_per_cluster, "child-weeks\n")
cat("Between-cluster CV:                    ", between_cluster_cv, "\n")
cat("Target power (two-sided):              ", target_power, "\n")
cat("Significance level (two-sided, α):     ", alpha, "\n")
cat("Allocation ratio (T:C):                 1:1 (equal allocation)\n\n")

cat("VARIANCE CALCULATION (CV Approximation)\n")
cat("-" %*% rep("-", 80), "\n")
cat("Formula: Var(rate) = [1 + k·μ·CV²] / (k·μ)\n")
cat("  where k = exposure per cluster, μ = expected events, CV = coefficient of variation\n\n")
cat("Treatment arm variance:                ", var_rate_t, "\n")
cat("  μ_t =", mu_t, "| 1 + 2500×12.5×0.0625 =", 1 + 2500*12.5*0.0625, "| ÷ 312.5 =", var_rate_t, "\n\n")
cat("Control arm variance:                  ", var_rate_c, "\n")
cat("  μ_c =", mu_c, "| 1 + 2500×25×0.0625 =", 1 + 2500*25*0.0625, "| ÷ 625 =", var_rate_c, "\n\n")

cat("CRITICAL VALUES (Two-sided)\n")
cat("-" %*% rep("-", 80), "\n")
cat("Z_{α/2} (upper, two-sided α=0.05):    ", z_alpha, "\n")
cat("Z_β (for 90% power):                   ", z_beta, "\n")
cat("Z_{α/2} + Z_β:                         ", z_alpha + z_beta, "\n\n")

cat("SAMPLE SIZE CALCULATION\n")
cat("-" %*% rep("-", 80), "\n")
cat("Formula: m = (Z_{α/2} + Z_β)² × (Var_t + Var_c) / (rate_diff)²\n\n")
m_continuous <- ((z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_rate_t + var_rate_c)) / (rate_diff^2)
cat("Continuous m (before correction):      ", round(m_continuous, 2), "\n")
cat("  = (", z_alpha + z_beta, ")² × (", var_rate_t, "+", var_rate_c, ") / (", rate_diff, ")²\n")
cat("  = ", (z_alpha + z_beta)^2, "×", var_rate_t + var_rate_c, "/", rate_diff^2, "\n")
cat("  = ", m_continuous, "\n\n")

cat("ADDITIVE ONE-CLUSTER CORRECTION\n")
cat("-" %*% rep("-", 80), "\n")
cat("(Finite-sample continuity adjustment per Hayes & Moulton)\n")
m_with_correction <- m_continuous + 1
cat("m with correction:                     ", m_with_correction, "\n\n")

cat("ROUNDING (upward to ensure ≥ target power)\n")
cat("-" %*% rep("-", 80), "\n")
m_rounded <- ceiling(m_with_correction)
cat("Clusters per arm (rounded up):         ", m_rounded, "\n")
cat("Total clusters:                        ", m_rounded * 2, "\n\n")

cat("ACHIEVED POWER VERIFICATION\n")
cat("-" %*% rep("-", 80), "\n")

# Power at selected design
var_diff_selected <- (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / m_rounded
se_diff_selected <- sqrt(var_diff_selected)
z_effect_selected <- rate_diff / se_diff_selected
power_selected <- pnorm(z_effect_selected - z_alpha) + pnorm(-z_effect_selected - z_alpha)

cat("At m =", m_rounded, "clusters per arm:\n")
cat("  SE(rate_diff) =", se_diff_selected, "\n")
cat("  Standardized effect (z_effect) =", z_effect_selected, "\n")
cat("  Achieved power =", round(power_selected, 6), "\n\n")

# Power at preceding design
if (m_rounded > 1) {
  m_prev <- m_rounded - 1
  var_diff_prev <- (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / m_prev
  se_diff_prev <- sqrt(var_diff_prev)
  z_effect_prev <- rate_diff / se_diff_prev
  power_prev <- pnorm(z_effect_prev - z_alpha) + pnorm(-z_effect_prev - z_alpha)
  
  cat("At m =", m_prev, "clusters per arm (preceding design):\n")
  cat("  SE(rate_diff) =", se_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("  Standardized effect (z_effect) =", z_effect_prev, "\n")
  cat("  Achieved power =", round(power_prev, 6), "\n\n")
}

cat("=" %*% rep("=", 80), "\n")
cat("FINAL ANSWER\n")
cat("=" %*% rep("=", 80), "\n")
cat("Sample size: ", m_rounded, " clusters per arm\n")

cat("=" %*% rep("=", 80), "\n")
