# Evidence e1; success=true

# Cluster-rate coefficient-of-variation approximation
# Field Trials of Health Interventions, Chapter 5, Section 6.1
# with additive one-cluster correction

# Parameters
treatment_rate <- 0.005  # per child-week
control_rate <- 0.010    # per child-week
exposure_per_cluster <- 2500  # child-weeks
between_cluster_cv <- 0.25    # dimensionless
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.90
allocation_ratio <- 1  # equal allocation

# Expected number of events per cluster (mean)
mu_t <- treatment_rate * exposure_per_cluster
mu_c <- control_rate * exposure_per_cluster

cat("Treatment rate (per child-week):", treatment_rate, "\n")
cat("Control rate (per child-week):", control_rate, "\n")
cat("Exposure per cluster (child-weeks):", exposure_per_cluster, "\n")
cat("Between-cluster CV:", between_cluster_cv, "\n")
cat("Expected events per cluster (treatment):", mu_t, "\n")
cat("Expected events per cluster (control):", mu_c, "\n\n")

# Two-sided critical value
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
z_beta <- qnorm(target_power)

cat("Two-sided alpha:", alpha, "\n")
cat("Target power:", target_power, "\n")
cat("Z-value for alpha/2 (1 - 0.025):", z_alpha, "\n")
cat("Z-value for power (", target_power, "):", z_beta, "\n\n")

# CV approximation formula for cluster-level rates
# The variance for cluster-level rate differences includes:
# 1. Poisson variation at individual level
# 2. Between-cluster variation captured via CV

# For equal allocation, the variance of rate difference is:
# Var(r_t - r_c) = Var(r_t) + Var(r_c)
# where Var(r) includes both Poisson and between-cluster components

# Under the CV approximation:
# Var(r_t) ≈ [mu_t + (mu_t * CV)^2] / exposure_per_cluster
# Var(r_c) ≈ [mu_c + (mu_c * CV)^2] / exposure_per_cluster

# For cluster-level aggregated data with Poisson base and gamma mixing:
# Variance includes: mu/exposure + (mu*CV)^2/exposure
# But the formula accounts for the between-cluster variance directly

# Using Hayes & Moulton formula for cluster-rate studies
# The effective variance for one cluster in each arm is:
# V_t = (1/mu_t + CV^2) / exposure_per_cluster  (approx. for treatment)
# V_c = (1/mu_c + CV^2) / exposure_per_cluster  (approx. for control)

# More precisely, for counts Y ~ negative binomial (Poisson-gamma mixture):
# Var(Y) = mu + (mu * CV)^2
# For rates, Var(rate) = Var(count) / exposure^2

# Hayes & Moulton Section 6.1 uses:
# Var of cluster rate = (1 + k*mu*CV^2) / (k*mu)
# where k is the number of observations per cluster (here: exposure_per_cluster)

k <- exposure_per_cluster

# Variance for treatment arm (per cluster)
var_rate_t <- (1 + k * mu_t * (between_cluster_cv^2)) / (k * mu_t)

# Variance for control arm (per cluster)
var_rate_c <- (1 + k * mu_c * (between_cluster_cv^2)) / (k * mu_c)

cat("Variance of cluster rate (treatment):", var_rate_t, "\n")
cat("Variance of cluster rate (control):", var_rate_c, "\n\n")

# Rate difference
rate_diff <- treatment_rate - control_rate
cat("Rate difference (treatment - control):", rate_diff, "\n\n")

# For equal allocation with m clusters per arm:
# Var(rate_diff) = var_rate_t/m + var_rate_c/m = (var_rate_t + var_rate_c)/m

# Sample size formula: m = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / (rate_diff)^2

m_continuous <- ((z_alpha + z_beta)^2 * (var_rate_t + var_rate_c)) / (rate_diff^2)

cat("Continuous sample size (clusters per arm, before correction):", m_continuous, "\n\n")

# Additive one-cluster correction (Hayes & Moulton)
# This is a finite-sample continuity adjustment
m_with_correction <- m_continuous + 1

cat("Sample size with one-cluster additive correction:", m_with_correction, "\n\n")

# Round upward to ensure power meets or exceeds target
m_rounded <- ceiling(m_with_correction)

cat("Sample size rounded upward (clusters per arm):", m_rounded, "\n")
cat("Total clusters:", m_rounded * 2, "\n\n")

# Verify achieved power at rounded design
# For verification, calculate power at m_rounded
m_check <- m_rounded

# Variance of rate difference with m_check clusters per arm
var_diff_check <- (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / m_check

# Standard error
se_diff_check <- sqrt(var_diff_check)

# Non-centrality parameter
ncp_check <- rate_diff / se_diff_check

# Achieved power (two-sided)
achieved_power <- 2 * pnorm(ncp_check - z_alpha) - 1

cat("Verification at m =", m_rounded, ":\n")
cat("Variance of rate difference:", var_diff_check, "\n")
cat("Standard error of rate difference:", se_diff_check, "\n")
cat("Non-centrality parameter:", ncp_check, "\n")
cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", round(achieved_power, 6), "\n\n")

# Also verify power at m_rounded - 1 to show rounding impact
if (m_rounded > 1) {
  m_prev <- m_rounded - 1
  var_diff_prev <- (var_rate_t + var_rate_c) / m_prev
  se_diff_prev <- sqrt(var_diff_prev)
  ncp_prev <- rate_diff / se_diff_prev
  achieved_power_prev <- 2 * pnorm(ncp_prev - z_alpha) - 1
  
  cat("Verification at m =", m_prev, "(preceding admissible design):\n")
  cat("Variance of rate difference:", var_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("Standard error of rate difference:", se_diff_prev, "\n")
  cat("Non-centrality parameter:", ncp_prev, "\n")
  cat("Achieved power (two-sided):", round(achieved_power_prev, 6), "\n\n")
}

# Final result
POWER_AGENT_RESULT=jsonlite::toJSON(list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "sample_size", value = m_rounded, unit = "clusters_per_arm"),
    list(metric = "achieved_power", value = round(achieved_power, 6), unit = "proportion")
  ),
  study_design = list(
    method = "cluster_rate_cv",

    between_cluster_cv = between_cluster_cv,

plan.estimand: Cumulative event probability difference under hazard ratio 0.7 in a log-rank test
plan.hypothesis: Two-sided comparison of survival curves via log-rank test: H0: HR = 1 vs H1: HR ≠ 1
assumptions: Two independent groups with proportional hazards
Log-rank test statistic follows normal approximation
Freedman approximation: power ≈ Φ(|log(HR)| × sqrt(D/4) − z_α/2) where D is total expected events
Equal allocation across treatment and control groups
No censoring pattern interaction with treatment assignment
scientific_notes: The Freedman approximation provides a closed-form power calculation for log-rank tests under the proportional hazards model
Event probabilities are assumed to be cumulative incidence by end of follow-up under the respective treatment arms

answer.summary: Using the Freedman approximation for log-rank tests as implemented in powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default, the power of a two-sided log-rank comparison with a hazard ratio of 0.7, event probabilities of 0.3707 (treatment) and 0.4890 (control), 200 participants per group, and α = 0.05 is **0.6383** (63.83%).
answer.method: Freedman approximation (Freedman 1982) for log-rank test under Cox proportional hazards model. The Freedman formula for two-sided testing with allocation ratio k = n_E/n_C is: power = Φ(√(k·m)·|RR−1|/(k·RR+1) − z_{1−α/2}), where m = n_E·p_E + n_C·p_C is the expected total number of events and Φ is the standard normal CDF. With m = 171.94 expected events and k = 1 (equal allocation), the Z-score for power is 0.354022, yielding power = Φ(0.354022) = 0.6383.
assumptions: Two independent groups with proportional hazards
Log-rank test statistic follows normal approximation
Freedman approximation valid under large-sample assumptions (central limit theorem applicable)
Event probabilities (0.3707 for treatment, 0.4890 for control) represent cumulative incidence by end of follow-up
Equal allocation across treatment and control groups (1:1 ratio)
No censoring pattern interaction with treatment assignment
Hazard ratio 0.7 reflects the true underlying effect
limitations: Freedman approximation assumes large sample size; validity confirmed with expected events m = 171.94
Event probabilities are assumed fixed and not estimated from data
Approximation assumes proportional hazards throughout follow-up
No adjustment for finite-sample effects or discrete nature of sample sizes

# Install and load powerSurvEpi package
if (!require("powerSurvEpi", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("powerSurvEpi", repos = "https://cran.r-project.org")
  library("powerSurvEpi")
}

# Define parameters per user request
alpha <- 0.05
hazard_ratio <- 0.7
event_prob_treatment <- 0.3707
event_prob_control <- 0.4890
n_treatment <- 200
n_control <- 200
allocation_ratio <- 1  # equal allocation

# Calculate power using powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default
# This function uses the Freedman approximation for log-rank test
power_result <- powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default(
  alpha = alpha,
  beta = NULL,  # We're computing power (1 - beta)
  hr = hazard_ratio,
  p0 = event_prob_control,
  p1 = event_prob_treatment,
  n = n_treatment,
  sided = 2
)

# Extract and display results
cat("Freedman Approximation - Log-Rank Test Power Calculation\n")
cat("========================================================\n")
cat(sprintf("Hazard ratio (HR): %.4f\n", hazard_ratio))
cat(sprintf("Event probability (treatment): %.4f\n", event_prob_treatment))
cat(sprintf("Event probability (control): %.4f\n", event_prob_control))
cat(sprintf("Sample size per group: %d\n", n_treatment))
cat(sprintf("Total sample size: %d\n", n_treatment + n_control))
cat(sprintf("Significance level (alpha): %.4f\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("Two-sided test\n"))
cat(sprintf("Equal allocation ratio\n\n"))

# Display the computed power
cat(sprintf("Computed Power: %.6f\n", power_result))

# Verify the computation by examining the underlying Freedman formula
# D = total expected events = n1*p1 + n0*p0
D_treatment <- n_treatment * event_prob_treatment
D_control <- n_control * event_prob_control
D_total <- D_treatment + D_control

cat(sprintf("\nFriedman Approximation Details:\n"))
cat(sprintf("Expected events (treatment): %.2f\n", D_treatment))
cat(sprintf("Expected events (control): %.2f\n", D_control))
cat(sprintf("Total expected events (D): %.2f\n", D_total))

# Freedman formula: power ≈ Φ(|log(HR)| × sqrt(D/4) − z_{α/2})
z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
log_hr <- log(hazard_ratio)
z_power <- abs(log_hr) * sqrt(D_total / 4) - z_alpha_2
computed_power <- pnorm(z_power)

cat(sprintf("log(HR): %.6f\n", log_hr))
cat(sprintf("z-statistic for α/2 = %.6f\n", z_alpha_2))
cat(sprintf("Z-score for power: %.6f\n", z_power))
cat(sprintf("Power from formula: %.6f\n", computed_power))

# Return result for structured reporting
library(jsonlite)
results <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "power", value = as.numeric(power_result), unit = "probability")
  ),
  simulation = NULL
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(results, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

     Power calculation for the Comparison of Survival Curves Between
     Two Groups under the Cox Proportional-Hazards Model for clinical
     trials. Some parameters will be estimated based on a pilot data

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     powerCT(formula, 
             dat,

             alpha = 0.05)
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

 formula: A formula object, e.g. ‘Surv(time, status) ~ x’, where ‘time’
          is a vector of survival/censoring time, ‘status’ is a vector
          of censoring indicator, ‘x’ is the group indicator, which is
          a factor object in R and takes only two possible values (‘C’
          for control group and ‘E’ for experimental group). See also
          the documentation of the function ‘survfit’ in the library
          ‘survival’.

     dat: a data frame representing the pilot data set and containing
          at least 3 columns: (1) survival/censoring time; (2)
          censoring indicator; (3) group indicator which is a factor
          object in R and takes only two possible values (‘C’ for
          control group and ‘E’ for experimental group).

      nE: integer. number of participants in the experimental group.

      nC: integer. number of participants in the control group.

      RR: numeric. postulated hazard ratio.

   alpha: numeric. type I error rate.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     This is an implementation of the power calculation method
     described in Section 14.12 (page 807) of Rosner (2006). The method
     was proposed by Freedman (1982).

     The movitation of this function is that some times we do not have
     information about m or p_E and p_C available, but we have a pilot
     data set that can be used to estimate p_E and p_C hence m, where
     m=n_E p_E + n_C p_C is the expected total number of events over
     both groups, n_E and n_C are numbers of participants in group E
     (experimental group) and group C (control group), respectively.
     p_E is the probability of failure in group E (experimental group)
     over the maximum time period of the study (t years).  p_C is the
     probability of failure in group C (control group) over the maximum
     time period of the study (t years).

     Suppose we want to compare the survival curves between an
     experimental group (E) and a control group (C) in a clinical trial
     with a maximum follow-up of t years.  The Cox proportional hazards
     regression model is assumed to have the form:

                      h(t|X_1)=h_0(t)\exp(beta_1 X_1).                  
     
     Let n_E be the number of participants in the E group and n_C be
     the number of participants in the C group.  We wish to test the
     hypothesis H0: RR=1 versus H1: RR not equal to 1, where
     RR=\exp(beta_1)=underlying hazard ratio for the E group versus the
     C group. Let RR be the postulated hazard ratio, alpha be the
     significance level. Assume that the test is a two-sided test. If
     the ratio of participants in group E compared to group C =
     n_E/n_C=k, then the power of the test is

             power=Phi(sqrt{k*m}*|RR-1|/(k*RR+1)-z_{1-alpha/2}),        
     
     where

                             m=n_E p_E+n_C p_C,                         
     
     and z_{1-alpha/2} is the 100 (1-alpha/2)-th percentile of the
     standard normal distribution N(0, 1), Phi is the cumulative
     distribution function (CDF) of N(0, 1).

     p_C and p_E can be calculated from the following formulaes:

                 p_C=sum_{i=1}^{t}D_i, p_E=sum_{i=1}^{t}E_i,            
     
     where D_i=lambda_i A_i C_i, E_i=RRlambda_i B_i C_i,
     A_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-lambda_j),
     B_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-RRlambda_j),
     C_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-delta_j).  And lambda_i is the probability
     of failure at time ‘i’ among participants in the control group,
     given that a participant has survived to time i-1 and is not
     censored at time i-1, i.e., the approximate hazard time i in the
     control group, i=1,...,t; RRlambda_i is the probability of failure
     at time ‘i’ among participants in the experimental group, given
     that a participant has survived to time i-1 and is not censored at
     time i-1, i.e., the approximate hazard time i in the experimental
     group, i=1,...,t; delta is the prbability that a participant is
     censored at time i given that he was followed up to time i and has
     not failed, i=0, 1, ..., t, which is assumed the same in each
     group.

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

mat.lambda: a matrix with 9 columns and ‘nTimes+1’ rows, where ‘nTimes’
          is the number of observed time points for the control group
          in the data set. The 9 columns are (1) ‘time’ - observed time
          point for the control group; (2) ‘lambda’; (3) ‘RRlambda’;
          (4) ‘delta’; (5) ‘A’; (6) ‘B’; (7) ‘C’; (8) ‘D’; (9) ‘E’.
          Please refer to the Details section for the definitions of
          elements of these quantities. See also Table 14.24 on page
          809 of Rosner (2006).

mat.event: a matrix with 5 columns and ‘nTimes+1’ rows, where ‘nTimes’
          is the number of observed time points for control group in
          the data set. The 5 columns are (1) ‘time’ - observed time
          point for the control group; (2) ‘nEvent.C’ - number of
          events in the control group at each time point; (3)
          ‘nCensored.C’ - number of censorings in the control group at
          each time point; (4) ‘nSurvive.C’ - number of alived in the
          control group at each time point; (5) ‘nRisk.C’ - number of
          participants at risk in the control group at each time point.
          Please refer to Table 14.12 on page 787 of Rosner (2006).

      pC: estimated probability of failure in group C (control group)
          over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      pE: estimated probability of failure in group E (experimental
          group) over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

   power: the power of the test.

_ N_ o_ t_ e:

     (1) The estimates of RRlambda_i=RR*lambda_i. That is, ‘RRlambda’
     is not directly estimated based on data from the experimental
     group; (2) The power formula assumes that the central-limit
     theorem is valid and hence is appropriate for large samples.

# Independent verification of the Freedman approximation
# Two-sided log-rank test with proportional hazards

# Given parameters
alpha <- 0.05
hazard_ratio <- 0.7
event_prob_E <- 0.3707  # experimental/treatment
event_prob_C <- 0.4890  # control
n_E <- 200
n_C <- 200

# Step 1: Calculate total expected events
m <- n_E * event_prob_E + n_C * event_prob_C
cat("Step 1: Expected number of events\n")
cat(sprintf("m = n_E * p_E + n_C * p_C\n"))
cat(sprintf("m = %d * %.4f + %d * %.4f = %.4f\n", 
            n_E, event_prob_E, n_C, event_prob_C, m))

# Step 2: Calculate allocation ratio
k <- n_E / n_C
cat(sprintf("\nAllocation ratio k = n_E / n_C = %.4f\n", k))

# Step 3: Calculate critical value for two-sided test
z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
cat(sprintf("\nStep 2: Critical value\n"))
cat(sprintf("z_{1-α/2} = qnorm(1 - %.2f/2) = %.6f\n", alpha, z_alpha_2))

# Step 4: Apply Freedman formula
# For two-sided test: power = Φ(sqrt(k*m) * |RR-1| / (k*RR + 1) - z_{1-α/2})
# Note: The formula uses RR - 1 in the numerator, not log(RR)

numerator_term <- sqrt(k * m) * abs(hazard_ratio - 1)
denominator_term <- k * hazard_ratio + 1
z_score <- numerator_term / denominator_term - z_alpha_2

cat(sprintf("\nStep 3: Freedman formula application\n"))
cat(sprintf("numerator = sqrt(k*m) * |HR-1| = sqrt(%.4f * %.4f) * |%.4f - 1| = %.6f\n",
            k, m, hazard_ratio, numerator_term))
cat(sprintf("denominator = k*HR + 1 = %.4f * %.4f + 1 = %.6f\n",
            k, hazard_ratio, denominator_term))
cat(sprintf("z-score = numerator/denominator - z_α/2 = %.6f / %.6f - %.6f = %.6f\n",
            numerator_term, denominator_term, z_alpha_2, z_score))

# Step 5: Calculate power
power <- pnorm(z_score)
cat(sprintf("\nStep 4: Power calculation\n"))
cat(sprintf("Power = Φ(z) = Φ(%.6f) = %.10f\n", z_score, power))

# Cross-check: verify against powerSurvEpi if available
cat("\n" %+% "="*60 %+% "\n")
cat("Cross-check with powerSurvEpi package:\n")

# Independent verification of the Freedman approximation
# Two-sided log-rank test with proportional hazards

# Given parameters
alpha <- 0.05
hazard_ratio <- 0.7
event_prob_E <- 0.3707  # experimental/treatment
event_prob_C <- 0.4890  # control
n_E <- 200
n_C <- 200

# Step 1: Calculate total expected events
m <- n_E * event_prob_E + n_C * event_prob_C
cat("Step 1: Expected number of events\n")
cat(sprintf("m = n_E * p_E + n_C * p_C\n"))
cat(sprintf("m = %d * %.4f + %d * %.4f = %.4f\n", 
            n_E, event_prob_E, n_C, event_prob_C, m))

# Step 2: Calculate allocation ratio
k <- n_E / n_C
cat(sprintf("\nAllocation ratio k = n_E / n_C = %.4f\n", k))

# Step 3: Calculate critical value for two-sided test
z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
cat(sprintf("\nStep 2: Critical value\n"))
cat(sprintf("z_{1-α/2} = qnorm(1 - %.2f/2) = %.6f\n", alpha, z_alpha_2))

# Step 4: Apply Freedman formula
# For two-sided test: power = Φ(sqrt(k*m) * |RR-1| / (k*RR + 1) - z_{1-α/2})
# Note: The formula uses RR - 1 in the numerator, not log(RR)

numerator_term <- sqrt(k * m) * abs(hazard_ratio - 1)
denominator_term <- k * hazard_ratio + 1
z_score <- numerator_term / denominator_term - z_alpha_2

cat(sprintf("\nStep 3: Freedman formula application\n"))
cat(sprintf("numerator = sqrt(k*m) * |HR-1| = sqrt(%.4f * %.4f) * |%.4f - 1| = %.6f\n",
            k, m, hazard_ratio, numerator_term))
cat(sprintf("denominator = k*HR + 1 = %.4f * %.4f + 1 = %.6f\n",
            k, hazard_ratio, denominator_term))
cat(sprintf("z-score = numerator/denominator - z_α/2 = %.6f / %.6f - %.6f = %.6f\n",
            numerator_term, denominator_term, z_alpha_2, z_score))

# Step 5: Calculate power
power <- pnorm(z_score)
cat(sprintf("\nStep 4: Power calculation\n"))
cat(sprintf("Power = Φ(z) = Φ(%.6f) = %.10f\n", z_score, power))

# Cross-check with powerSurvEpi
cat("\n")
cat(paste(rep("=", 60), collapse=""))
cat("\nCross-check with powerSurvEpi package:\n")
cat(paste(rep("=", 60), collapse=""))
cat("\n")

if (require("powerSurvEpi", quietly = TRUE)) {
  power_pkg <- powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default(
    nE = n_E,
    nC = n_C,
    pE = event_prob_E,
    pC = event_prob_C,
    RR = hazard_ratio,
    alpha = alpha
  )
  cat(sprintf("powerSurvEpi result:  %.15f\n", power_pkg))
  cat(sprintf("Manual calculation:  %.15f\n", power))
  cat(sprintf("Absolute difference: %.2e\n", abs(power - power_pkg)))
  
  if (isTRUE(all.equal(power, power_pkg, tolerance = 1e-10))) {
    cat("VERIFICATION: PASS - Results match within numerical precision\n")
  } else {
    cat("VERIFICATION: FAIL - Results differ significantly\n")
  }
} else {
  cat("powerSurvEpi not available for cross-check\n")
}

# Return structured result
library(jsonlite)
results <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "power", value = power, unit = "probability")
  ),
  simulation = NULL
)

cat("\n\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(results, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

# Install and load powerSurvEpi package
if (!require("powerSurvEpi", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("powerSurvEpi", repos = "https://cran.r-project.org")
  library("powerSurvEpi")
}

# Define parameters per user request
alpha <- 0.05
hazard_ratio <- 0.7
event_prob_treatment <- 0.3707
event_prob_control <- 0.4890
n_treatment <- 200
n_control <- 200
allocation_ratio <- 1  # equal allocation

# Calculate power using powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default
# This function uses the Freedman approximation for log-rank test
power_result <- powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default(
  alpha = alpha,
  beta = NULL,  # We're computing power (1 - beta)
  hr = hazard_ratio,
  p0 = event_prob_control,
  p1 = event_prob_treatment,
  n = n_treatment,
  sided = 2
)

# Extract and display results
cat("Freedman Approximation - Log-Rank Test Power Calculation\n")
cat("========================================================\n")
cat(sprintf("Hazard ratio (HR): %.4f\n", hazard_ratio))
cat(sprintf("Event probability (treatment): %.4f\n", event_prob_treatment))
cat(sprintf("Event probability (control): %.4f\n", event_prob_control))
cat(sprintf("Sample size per group: %d\n", n_treatment))
cat(sprintf("Total sample size: %d\n", n_treatment + n_control))
cat(sprintf("Significance level (alpha): %.4f\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("Two-sided test\n"))
cat(sprintf("Equal allocation ratio\n\n"))

# Display the computed power
cat(sprintf("Computed Power: %.6f\n", power_result))

# Verify the computation by examining the underlying Freedman formula
# D = total expected events = n1*p1 + n0*p0
D_treatment <- n_treatment * event_prob_treatment
D_control <- n_control * event_prob_control
D_total <- D_treatment + D_control

cat(sprintf("\nFriedman Approximation Details:\n"))
cat(sprintf("Expected events (treatment): %.2f\n", D_treatment))
cat(sprintf("Expected events (control): %.2f\n", D_control))
cat(sprintf("Total expected events (D): %.2f\n", D_total))

# Freedman formula: power ≈ Φ(|log(HR)| × sqrt(D/4) − z_{α/2})
z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
log_hr <- log(hazard_ratio)
z_power <- abs(log_hr) * sqrt(D_total / 4) - z_alpha_2
computed_power <- pnorm(z_power)

cat(sprintf("log(HR): %.6f\n", log_hr))
cat(sprintf("z-statistic for α/2 = %.6f\n", z_alpha_2))
cat(sprintf("Z-score for power: %.6f\n", z_power))
cat(sprintf("Power from formula: %.6f\n", computed_power))

# Return result for structured reporting
library(jsonlite)
results <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "power", value = as.numeric(power_result), unit = "probability")
  ),
  simulation = NULL
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(results, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

 formula: A formula object, e.g. ‘Surv(time, status) ~ x’, where ‘time’

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     This is an implementation of the power calculation method
     described in Section 14.12 (page 807) of Rosner (2006). The method
     was proposed by Freedman (1982).

     The movitation of this function is that some times we do not have
     information about m or p_E and p_C available, but we have a pilot
     data set that can be used to estimate p_E and p_C hence m, where
     m=n_E p_E + n_C p_C is the expected total number of events over
     both groups, n_E and n_C are numbers of participants in group E
     (experimental group) and group C (control group), respectively.
     p_E is the probability of failure in group E (experimental group)
     over the maximum time period of the study (t years).  p_C is the
     probability of failure in group C (control group) over the maximum
     time period of the study (t years).

     Suppose we want to compare the survival curves between an
     experimental group (E) and a control group (C) in a clinical trial
     with a maximum follow-up of t years.  The Cox proportional hazards
     regression model is assumed to have the form:

                      h(t|X_1)=h_0(t)\exp(beta_1 X_1).                  
     
     Let n_E be the number of participants in the E group and n_C be
     the number of participants in the C group.  We wish to test the
     hypothesis H0: RR=1 versus H1: RR not equal to 1, where
     RR=\exp(beta_1)=underlying hazard ratio for the E group versus the
     C group. Let RR be the postulated hazard ratio, alpha be the
     significance level. Assume that the test is a two-sided test. If
     the ratio of participants in group E compared to group C =
     n_E/n_C=k, then the power of the test is

             power=Phi(sqrt{k*m}*|RR-1|/(k*RR+1)-z_{1-alpha/2}),        
     
     where

                             m=n_E p_E+n_C p_C,                         
     
     and z_{1-alpha/2} is the 100 (1-alpha/2)-th percentile of the
     standard normal distribution N(0, 1), Phi is the cumulative
     distribution function (CDF) of N(0, 1).

     p_C and p_E can be calculated from the following formulaes:

                 p_C=sum_{i=1}^{t}D_i, p_E=sum_{i=1}^{t}E_i,            
     
     where D_i=lambda_i A_i C_i, E_i=RRlambda_i B_i C_i,
     A_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-lambda_j),
     B_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-RRlambda_j),
     C_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-delta_j).  And lambda_i is the probability
     of failure at time ‘i’ among participants in the control group,
     given that a participant has survived to time i-1 and is not
     censored at time i-1, i.e., the approximate hazard time i in the
     control group, i=1,...,t; RRlambda_i is the probability of failure
     at time ‘i’ among participants in the experimental group, given
     that a participant has survived to time i-1 and is not censored at
     time i-1, i.e., the approximate hazard time i in the experimental
     group, i=1,...,t; delta is the prbability that a participant is
     censored at time i given that he was followed up to time i and has
     not failed, i=0, 1, ..., t, which is assumed the same in each
     group.

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

mat.lambda: a matrix with 9 columns and ‘nTimes+1’ rows, where ‘nTimes’
          is the number of observed time points for the control group
          in the data set. The 9 columns are (1) ‘time’ - observed time
          point for the control group; (2) ‘lambda’; (3) ‘RRlambda’;
          (4) ‘delta’; (5) ‘A’; (6) ‘B’; (7) ‘C’; (8) ‘D’; (9) ‘E’.
          Please refer to the Details section for the definitions of
          elements of these quantities. See also Table 14.24 on page
          809 of Rosner (2006).

mat.event: a matrix with 5 columns and ‘nTimes+1’ rows, where ‘nTimes’
          is the number of observed time points for control group in
          the data set. The 5 columns are (1) ‘time’ - observed time
          point for the control group; (2) ‘nEvent.C’ - number of
          events in the control group at each time point; (3)
          ‘nCensored.C’ - number of censorings in the control group at
          each time point; (4) ‘nSurvive.C’ - number of alived in the
          control group at each time point; (5) ‘nRisk.C’ - number of
          participants at risk in the control group at each time point.
          Please refer to Table 14.12 on page 787 of Rosner (2006).

      pC: estimated probability of failure in group C (control group)
          over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      pE: estimated probability of failure in group E (experimental
          group) over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

   power: the power of the test.

_ N_ o_ t_ e:

     (1) The estimates of RRlambda_i=RR*lambda_i. That is, ‘RRlambda’
     is not directly estimated based on data from the experimental
     group; (2) The power formula assumes that the central-limit
     theorem is valid and hence is appropriate for large samples.

# Load packages
library("powerSurvEpi")
library("jsonlite")

# Define parameters per user request
alpha <- 0.05
hazard_ratio <- 0.7  # RR in the function
event_prob_treatment <- 0.3707  # pE
event_prob_control <- 0.4890    # pC
n_treatment <- 200   # nE
n_control <- 200     # nC

# According to the function signature, powerCT.default takes:
# (nE, nC, pE, pC, RR, alpha = 0.05)
power_result <- powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default(
  nE = n_treatment,
  nC = n_control,
  pE = event_prob_treatment,
  pC = event_prob_control,
  RR = hazard_ratio,
  alpha = alpha
)

# Display results
cat("Freedman Approximation - Log-Rank Test Power Calculation\n")
cat("========================================================\n")
cat(sprintf("Hazard ratio (HR): %.4f\n", hazard_ratio))
cat(sprintf("Event probability (treatment): %.4f\n", event_prob_treatment))
cat(sprintf("Event probability (control): %.4f\n", event_prob_control))
cat(sprintf("Sample size (experimental group): %d\n", n_treatment))
cat(sprintf("Sample size (control group): %d\n", n_control))
cat(sprintf("Total sample size: %d\n", n_treatment + n_control))
cat(sprintf("Significance level (alpha): %.4f\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("Two-sided test\n"))
cat(sprintf("Equal allocation ratio: 1\n\n"))

# Display the computed power
cat(sprintf("Computed Power: %.6f\n", power_result))

# Verify the computation by examining the underlying Freedman formula
# m = n_E * p_E + n_C * p_C (total expected events)
m <- n_treatment * event_prob_treatment + n_control * event_prob_control
k <- n_treatment / n_control  # allocation ratio

# Freedman formula for two-sided test:
# power = Φ(sqrt(k*m) * |RR-1| / (k*RR + 1) - z_{1-α/2})
z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
z_power <- sqrt(k * m) * abs(hazard_ratio - 1) / (k * hazard_ratio + 1) - z_alpha_2
computed_power_manual <- pnorm(z_power)

cat(sprintf("\nFriedman Formula Verification:\n"))
cat(sprintf("Total expected events (m): %.2f\n", m))
cat(sprintf("Allocation ratio (k = nE/nC): %.4f\n", k))
cat(sprintf("z-critical (z_{1-α/2}): %.6f\n", z_alpha_2))
cat(sprintf("Numerator: sqrt(k*m) * |RR-1| = %.6f\n", sqrt(k*m) * abs(hazard_ratio - 1)))
cat(sprintf("Denominator: k*RR + 1 = %.6f\n", k * hazard_ratio + 1))
cat(sprintf("Z-score for power: %.6f\n", z_power))
cat(sprintf("Power (from formula): %.6f\n", computed_power_manual))

# Return result for structured reporting
results <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "power", value = as.numeric(power_result), unit = "probability")
  ),
  simulation = NULL
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(results, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

# Independent verification of the Freedman approximation
# Two-sided log-rank test with proportional hazards

# Given parameters
alpha <- 0.05
hazard_ratio <- 0.7
event_prob_E <- 0.3707  # experimental/treatment
event_prob_C <- 0.4890  # control
n_E <- 200
n_C <- 200

# Step 1: Calculate total expected events
m <- n_E * event_prob_E + n_C * event_prob_C
cat("Step 1: Expected number of events\n")
cat(sprintf("m = n_E * p_E + n_C * p_C\n"))
cat(sprintf("m = %d * %.4f + %d * %.4f = %.4f\n", 
            n_E, event_prob_E, n_C, event_prob_C, m))

# Step 2: Calculate allocation ratio
k <- n_E / n_C
cat(sprintf("\nAllocation ratio k = n_E / n_C = %.4f\n", k))

# Step 3: Calculate critical value for two-sided test
z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
cat(sprintf("\nStep 2: Critical value\n"))
cat(sprintf("z_{1-α/2} = qnorm(1 - %.2f/2) = %.6f\n", alpha, z_alpha_2))

# Step 4: Apply Freedman formula
# For two-sided test: power = Φ(sqrt(k*m) * |RR-1| / (k*RR + 1) - z_{1-α/2})
# Note: The formula uses RR - 1 in the numerator, not log(RR)

numerator_term <- sqrt(k * m) * abs(hazard_ratio - 1)
denominator_term <- k * hazard_ratio + 1
z_score <- numerator_term / denominator_term - z_alpha_2

cat(sprintf("\nStep 3: Freedman formula application\n"))
cat(sprintf("numerator = sqrt(k*m) * |HR-1| = sqrt(%.4f * %.4f) * |%.4f - 1| = %.6f\n",
            k, m, hazard_ratio, numerator_term))
cat(sprintf("denominator = k*HR + 1 = %.4f * %.4f + 1 = %.6f\n",
            k, hazard_ratio, denominator_term))
cat(sprintf("z-score = numerator/denominator - z_α/2 = %.6f / %.6f - %.6f = %.6f\n",
            numerator_term, denominator_term, z_alpha_2, z_score))

# Step 5: Calculate power
power <- pnorm(z_score)
cat(sprintf("\nStep 4: Power calculation\n"))
cat(sprintf("Power = Φ(z) = Φ(%.6f) = %.10f\n", z_score, power))

# Cross-check: verify against powerSurvEpi if available
cat("\n" %+% "="*60 %+% "\n")
cat("Cross-check with powerSurvEpi package:\n")
cat("="*60 %+% "\n")

if (require("powerSurvEpi", quietly = TRUE)) {
  power_pkg <- powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default(
    nE = n_E,
    nC = n_C,
    pE = event_prob_E,
    pC = event_prob_C,
    RR = hazard_ratio,
    alpha = alpha
  )
  cat(sprintf("powerSurvEpi result: %.10f\n", power_pkg))
  cat(sprintf("Manual calculation: %.10f\n", power))
  cat(sprintf("Difference: %.2e\n", abs(power - power_pkg)))
  cat(sprintf("Match: %s\n", isTRUE(all.equal(power, power_pkg, tolerance = 1e-6))))
} else {
  cat("powerSurvEpi not available for cross-check\n")
}

# Return structured result
library(jsonlite)
results <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "power", value = power, unit = "probability")
  ),
  simulation = NULL
)

cat("\n\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(results, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

# Check the Freedman formula more carefully
# The candidate answer claims: power ≈ Φ(√(k·m)·|RR−1|/(k·RR+1) − z_{1−α/2})
# But some literature uses log(RR) instead of RR-1
# Let's verify which is correct by checking the Rosner/Freedman reference

cat("Freedman Formula Analysis\n")
cat("="*60 %+% "\n", sep="")
cat("\nFormulation 1: Using (RR - 1) [As used in powerSurvEpi]\n")
cat("power = Φ(sqrt(k*m) * |RR-1| / (k*RR + 1) - z_{1-α/2})\n\n")

# Given parameters
alpha <- 0.05
HR <- 0.7
pE <- 0.3707
pC <- 0.4890
nE <- 200
nC <- 200
m <- nE*pE + nC*pC
k <- nE/nC
z_crit <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)

# Formula 1
z_score_1 <- sqrt(k*m) * abs(HR - 1) / (k*HR + 1) - z_crit
power_1 <- pnorm(z_score_1)
cat(sprintf("z-score (Formula 1): %.6f\n", z_score_1))
cat(sprintf("Power (Formula 1):   %.10f\n\n", power_1))

cat("Formulation 2: Using log(RR) [Alternative in some literature]\n")
cat("power = Φ(sqrt(k*m) * |log(RR)| / sqrt(4) - z_{1-α/2})\n")
cat("       = Φ(sqrt(k*m/4) * |log(RR)| - z_{1-α/2})\n\n")

# Formula 2
z_score_2 <- sqrt(k*m/4) * abs(log(HR)) - z_crit
power_2 <- pnorm(z_score_2)
cat(sprintf("z-score (Formula 2): %.6f\n", z_score_2))
cat(sprintf("Power (Formula 2):   %.10f\n\n", power_2))

cat("Which formula is implemented in powerSurvEpi?\n")
cat("Since our manual calculation using Formula 1 matches powerSurvEpi exactly,\n")
cat("powerSurvEpi uses: power = Φ(sqrt(k*m) * |RR-1| / (k*RR + 1) - z_{1-α/2})\n\n")

# Now test power under null hypothesis (HR=1)
cat("="*60 %+% "\n", sep="")
cat("\nNull Hypothesis Test (HR = 1 should give power ≈ α)\n")
cat("="*60 %+% "\n\n")

HR_null <- 1.0
z_score_null <- sqrt(k*m) * abs(HR_null - 1) / (k*HR_null + 1) - z_crit
power_null <- pnorm(z_score_null)

cat(sprintf("Under H0: HR = %.1f\n", HR_null))
cat(sprintf("z-score: %.6f\n", z_score_null))
cat(sprintf("Power: %.6f\n", power_null))
cat(sprintf("Expected: α = %.4f\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("Match: %s\n\n", abs(power_null - alpha) < 0.001))

# Return structured result
library(jsonlite)
results <- list(
  results = list(
    list(metric = "power", value = power_1, unit = "probability")
  ),
  simulation = NULL
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(toJSON(results, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15))

# Formula 2

power_2 <- pnorm(z_score_2)
cat(sprintf("z-score (Formula 2): %.6f\n", z_score_2))

cat("Null Hypothesis Test (HR = 1 should give power ≈ α)\n")
cat(strrep("=", 60), "\n\n")

     Power calculation for the Comparison of Survival Curves Between
     Two Groups under the Cox Proportional-Hazards Model for clinical

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     powerCT(formula, 
             dat,

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

 formula: A formula object, e.g. ‘Surv(time, status) ~ x’, where ‘time’
          is a vector of survival/censoring time, ‘status’ is a vector
          of censoring indicator, ‘x’ is the group indicator, which is
          a factor object in R and takes only two possible values (‘C’
          for control group and ‘E’ for experimental group). See also
          the documentation of the function ‘survfit’ in the library
          ‘survival’.

     dat: a data frame representing the pilot data set and containing
          at least 3 columns: (1) survival/censoring time; (2)
          censoring indicator; (3) group indicator which is a factor
          object in R and takes only two possible values (‘C’ for
          control group and ‘E’ for experimental group).

      nC: integer. number of participants in the control group.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     This is an implementation of the power calculation method
     described in Section 14.12 (page 807) of Rosner (2006). The method
     was proposed by Freedman (1982).

     The movitation of this function is that some times we do not have
     information about m or p_E and p_C available, but we have a pilot
     data set that can be used to estimate p_E and p_C hence m, where
     m=n_E p_E + n_C p_C is the expected total number of events over
     both groups, n_E and n_C are numbers of participants in group E
     (experimental group) and group C (control group), respectively.
     p_E is the probability of failure in group E (experimental group)
     over the maximum time period of the study (t years).  p_C is the
     probability of failure in group C (control group) over the maximum
     time period of the study (t years).

     Suppose we want to compare the survival curves between an
     experimental group (E) and a control group (C) in a clinical trial
     with a maximum follow-up of t years.  The Cox proportional hazards
     regression model is assumed to have the form:

                      h(t|X_1)=h_0(t)\exp(beta_1 X_1).                  
     
     Let n_E be the number of participants in the E group and n_C be
     the number of participants in the C group.  We wish to test the
     hypothesis H0: RR=1 versus H1: RR not equal to 1, where
     RR=\exp(beta_1)=underlying hazard ratio for the E group versus the
     C group. Let RR be the postulated hazard ratio, alpha be the
     significance level. Assume that the test is a two-sided test. If
     the ratio of participants in group E compared to group C =
     n_E/n_C=k, then the power of the test is

             power=Phi(sqrt{k*m}*|RR-1|/(k*RR+1)-z_{1-alpha/2}),        
     
     where

                             m=n_E p_E+n_C p_C,                         
     
     and z_{1-alpha/2} is the 100 (1-alpha/2)-th percentile of the
     standard normal distribution N(0, 1), Phi is the cumulative
     distribution function (CDF) of N(0, 1).

     p_C and p_E can be calculated from the following formulaes:

                 p_C=sum_{i=1}^{t}D_i, p_E=sum_{i=1}^{t}E_i,            
     
     where D_i=lambda_i A_i C_i, E_i=RRlambda_i B_i C_i,
     A_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-lambda_j),
     B_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-RRlambda_j),
     C_i=prod_{j=0}^{i-1}(1-delta_j).  And lambda_i is the probability
     of failure at time ‘i’ among participants in the control group,
     given that a participant has survived to time i-1 and is not
     censored at time i-1, i.e., the approximate hazard time i in the
     control group, i=1,...,t; RRlambda_i is the probability of failure
     at time ‘i’ among participants in the experimental group, given
     that a participant has survived to time i-1 and is not censored at
     time i-1, i.e., the approximate hazard time i in the experimental
     group, i=1,...,t; delta is the prbability that a participant is
     censored at time i given that he was followed up to time i and has
     not failed, i=0, 1, ..., t, which is assumed the same in each
     group.

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

mat.lambda: a matrix with 9 columns and ‘nTimes+1’ rows, where ‘nTimes’
          is the number of observed time points for the control group
          in the data set. The 9 columns are (1) ‘time’ - observed time
          point for the control group; (2) ‘lambda’; (3) ‘RRlambda’;
          (4) ‘delta’; (5) ‘A’; (6) ‘B’; (7) ‘C’; (8) ‘D’; (9) ‘E’.
          Please refer to the Details section for the definitions of
          elements of these quantities. See also Table 14.24 on page
          809 of Rosner (2006).

mat.event: a matrix with 5 columns and ‘nTimes+1’ rows, where ‘nTimes’
          is the number of observed time points for control group in
          the data set. The 5 columns are (1) ‘time’ - observed time
          point for the control group; (2) ‘nEvent.C’ - number of
          events in the control group at each time point; (3)
          ‘nCensored.C’ - number of censorings in the control group at
          each time point; (4) ‘nSurvive.C’ - number of alived in the
          control group at each time point; (5) ‘nRisk.C’ - number of
          participants at risk in the control group at each time point.
          Please refer to Table 14.12 on page 787 of Rosner (2006).

      pC: estimated probability of failure in group C (control group)
          over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      pE: estimated probability of failure in group E (experimental
          group) over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

   power: the power of the test.

_ N_ o_ t_ e:

     (1) The estimates of RRlambda_i=RR*lambda_i. That is, ‘RRlambda’
     is not directly estimated based on data from the experimental
     group; (2) The power formula assumes that the central-limit
     theorem is valid and hence is appropriate for large samples.

Freedman approximation applies: uses average event probability and assumes asymptotic normality of log-rank test statistic

scientific_notes: Freedman (1982) approximation: n = (z_alpha + z_beta)² / [p(1−p)(log(HR))²], where p is the overall event probability averaged across arms

answer.summary: Using the Freedman (1982) approximation for a two-sided log-rank test with α = 0.05, target power = 0.80, hazard ratio = 0.70, event probabilities 0.3707 (treatment) and 0.4890 (control), and 1:1 allocation, the required sample size is 294 participants per group (588 total). This calculation was performed using powerSurvEpi::ssizeCT.default, which implements the full Freedman formula accounting for unequal event probabilities across arms.
answer.method: Freedman (1982) approximation for log-rank test sample size, as implemented in powerSurvEpi::ssizeCT.default (Rosner 2006 Example 14.42). The formula is: m = (1/k)×((k×RR+1)/(RR-1))²×(z₁₋α/₂ + z₁₋β)², with per-group sample sizes n_E = n_C = m×k/(k×pE + pC), rounded up to integers.
assumptions: Two-arm parallel design with equal allocation (k = 1:1)
Two-sided log-rank test hypothesis: H₀: HR = 1 vs H₁: HR ≠ 1
Proportional hazards assumption holds
Event probabilities 0.3707 (treatment) and 0.4890 (control) are marginal probabilities over the study follow-up period
Type I error rate α = 0.05 (two-sided critical value z₁₋α/₂ = 1.960)
Target power 1 - β = 0.80 (one-sided critical value z₁₋β = 0.842)
Central limit theorem is valid for large sample sizes
Hazard ratio 0.70 is the postulated effect magnitude
limitations: The Freedman approximation assumes asymptotic normality and is most accurate for large sample sizes
Actual power depends on realized event rates in the trial; specified event probabilities are design assumptions
No inflation for loss to follow-up or other attrition; the event probabilities should incorporate anticipated follow-up
The formula applies to the log-rank test; other test statistics may require different sample sizes
Rounding to integer (294) may yield slightly higher power than exactly 0.80

# Two-sided log-rank test sample size: Freedman approximation
# powerSurvEpi::ssizeCT.default equivalent calculation

# Input parameters
alpha <- 0.05                  # two-sided significance level
power <- 0.80                  # target power
p_treatment <- 0.3707          # event probability in treatment arm
p_control <- 0.4890            # event probability in control arm
hr <- 0.7                      # hazard ratio
allocation_ratio <- 1          # 1:1 allocation

# Critical values
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)  # two-sided alpha cutoff
z_beta <- qnorm(power)         # one-sided power cutoff

# Overall (average) event probability
p <- (p_treatment + p_control) / 2

# Log hazard ratio
log_hr <- log(hr)

# Freedman approximation formula for per-group sample size
# n = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / [p(1-p)(log(HR))^2]
n_continuous <- (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / (p * (1 - p) * (log_hr)^2)

# Integer sample size (ceiling for per-group count)
n_integer <- ceiling(n_continuous)

cat("=== Freedman Approximation for Log-Rank Test (Two-sided) ===\n")
cat("\nInput Parameters:\n")
cat(sprintf("  Significance level (alpha):        %.4f\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("  Target power:                      %.2f\n", power))
cat(sprintf("  Hazard ratio:                      %.2f\n", hr))
cat(sprintf("  Event probability (treatment):     %.4f\n", p_treatment))
cat(sprintf("  Event probability (control):       %.4f\n", p_control))
cat(sprintf("  Allocation ratio:                  1:1\n"))

cat("\nCalculation:\n")
cat(sprintf("  z_alpha (two-sided):               %.6f\n", z_alpha))
cat(sprintf("  z_beta (one-sided):                %.6f\n", z_beta))
cat(sprintf("  Average event probability (p):     %.6f\n", p))
cat(sprintf("  Log(hazard ratio):                 %.6f\n", log_hr))
cat(sprintf("  p(1-p):                            %.6f\n", p * (1 - p)))
cat(sprintf("  (log(HR))^2:                       %.6f\n", (log_hr)^2))

cat("\nResults:\n")
cat(sprintf("  Continuous sample size per group:  %.2f\n", n_continuous))
cat(sprintf("  Integer sample size per group:     %d\n", n_integer))
cat(sprintf("  Total sample size (both arms):     %d\n", 2 * n_integer))

# Store results for output
results <- list(
  metric = "sample_size",
  value = n_integer,
  unit = "participants_per_group",
  continuous_estimate = n_continuous
)

print(results)

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     Sample size calculation for the Comparison of Survival Curves
     Between Two Groups under the Cox Proportional-Hazards Model for
     clinical trials.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     ssizeCT.default(power, 
                     k, 
                     pE, 
                     pC, 
                     RR, 
                     alpha = 0.05)
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

   power: numeric. power to detect the magnitude of the hazard ratio as
          small as that specified by ‘RR’.

       k: numeric. ratio of participants in group E (experimental
          group) compared to group C (control group).

      pE: numeric. probability of failure in group E (experimental
          group) over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      pC: numeric. probability of failure in group C (control group)
          over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      RR: numeric. postulated hazard ratio.

   alpha: numeric. type I error rate.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     This is an implementation of the sample size calculation method
     described in Section 14.12 (page 807) of Rosner (2006). The method
     was proposed by Freedman (1982).

     Suppose we want to compare the survival curves between an
     experimental group (E) and a control group (C) in a clinical trial
     with a maximum follow-up of t years.  The Cox proportional hazards
     regression model is assumed to have the form:

                      h(t|X_1)=h_0(t)\exp(beta_1 X_1).                  
     
     Let n_E be the number of participants in the E group and n_C be
     the number of participants in the C group.  We wish to test the
     hypothesis H0: RR=1 versus H1: RR not equal to 1, where
     RR=\exp(beta_1)=underlying hazard ratio for the E group versus the
     C group. Let RR be the postulated hazard ratio, alpha be the
     significance level. Assume that the test is a two-sided test. If
     the ratio of participants in group E compared to group C =
     n_E/n_C=k, then the number of participants needed in each group to
     achieve a power of 1-beta is

           n_E=\frac{m k}{k p_E + p_C}, n_C=\frac{m}{k p_E + p_C}       
     
     where

     m=\frac{1}{k}<=ft(\frac{k RR + 1}{RR - 1}\right)^2<=ft(
     z_{1-alpha/2}+z_{1-beta}
     \right)^2,
     
     and z_{1-alpha/2} is the 100 (1-alpha/2)-th percentile of the
     standard normal distribution N(0, 1).

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

     A two-element vector. The first element is n_E and the second
     element is n_C.

_ N_ o_ t_ e:

     (1) The sample size formula assumes that the central-limit theorem
     is valid and hence is appropriate for large samples. (2) n_E and
     n_C will be rounded up to integers.

_ R_ e_ f_ e_ r_ e_ n_ c_ e_ s:

     Freedman, L.S. (1982).  Tables of the number of patients required
     in clinical trials using the log-rank test.  _Statistics in
     Medicine_. 1: 121-129

library("powerSurvEpi")

# Re-create the Freedman formula as documented in powerSurvEpi help
# The documentation states:
# m = (1/k) * ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2 * (z_{1-alpha/2} + z_{1-beta})^2
# n_E = m*k / (k*p_E + p_C)
# n_C = m / (k*p_E + p_C)

power <- 0.80
k <- 1          # allocation ratio
pE <- 0.3707    # event prob experimental
pC <- 0.4890    # event prob control
RR <- 0.7       # hazard ratio (relative risk)
alpha <- 0.05

# Critical values
z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)    # two-sided
z_beta <- qnorm(power)              # one-sided

cat("=== Detailed Freedman Formula from powerSurvEpi Documentation ===\n\n")
cat(sprintf("Parameters:\n"))
cat(sprintf("  power = %.2f\n", power))
cat(sprintf("  k (allocation) = %.1f\n", k))
cat(sprintf("  pE = %.4f\n", pE))
cat(sprintf("  pC = %.4f\n", pC))
cat(sprintf("  RR = %.2f\n", RR))
cat(sprintf("  alpha = %.4f\n", alpha))

cat(sprintf("\nCritical values:\n"))
cat(sprintf("  z_{1-alpha/2} = %.6f\n", z_alpha_2))
cat(sprintf("  z_{1-beta} = %.6f\n", z_beta))
cat(sprintf("  z_{1-alpha/2} + z_{1-beta} = %.6f\n", z_alpha_2 + z_beta))

# Step 1: Calculate m
m_numerator <- (k * RR + 1)^2
m_denominator <- (RR - 1)^2
m_factor <- (1/k) * (m_numerator / m_denominator) * (z_alpha_2 + z_beta)^2

cat(sprintf("\nStep 1: Calculate m\n"))
cat(sprintf("  (k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1) = (%.1f*%.2f + 1)/(%.2f - 1) = (%.4f)/(%.4f) = %.6f\n",
    k, RR, RR, k*RR + 1, RR - 1, (k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1)))
cat(sprintf("  ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2 = %.6f\n", ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2))
cat(sprintf("  (1/k) * ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2 * (z_1-alpha/2 + z_1-beta)^2\n"))
cat(sprintf("  = (1/%.1f) * %.6f * %.6f\n", k, ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2, (z_alpha_2 + z_beta)^2))
cat(sprintf("  m = %.6f\n", m_factor))

# Step 2: Calculate n_E and n_C
denominator_common <- k * pE + pC

n_E <- m_factor * k / denominator_common
n_C <- m_factor / denominator_common

cat(sprintf("\nStep 2: Calculate sample sizes\n"))
cat(sprintf("  k*pE + pC = %.1f*%.4f + %.4f = %.6f\n", k, pE, pC, denominator_common))
cat(sprintf("  n_E = m*k / (k*pE + pC) = %.6f*%.1f / %.6f = %.6f → %d\n", 
    m_factor, k, denominator_common, n_E, ceiling(n_E)))
cat(sprintf("  n_C = m / (k*pE + pC) = %.6f / %.6f = %.6f → %d\n", 
    m_factor, denominator_common, n_C, ceiling(n_C)))

cat(sprintf("\n=== Comparison with Simple Formula ===\n"))
cat("Simple formula (what we used initially):\n")
cat("  n = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / [p(1-p)(log(RR))^2]\n")
cat("  where p = (pE + pC)/2\n")

p_avg <- (pE + pC) / 2
log_rr <- log(RR)
n_simple <- (z_alpha_2 + z_beta)^2 / (p_avg * (1 - p_avg) * (log_rr)^2)

cat(sprintf("\n  p_avg = (%.4f + %.4f)/2 = %.6f\n", pE, pC, p_avg))
cat(sprintf("  log(RR) = log(%.2f) = %.6f\n", RR, log_rr))
cat(sprintf("  n_simple = (%.6f)^2 / (%.6f * %.6f * (%.6f)^2)\n",
    z_alpha_2 + z_beta, p_avg, 1 - p_avg, log_rr))
cat(sprintf("  n_simple = %.6f → %d\n", n_simple, ceiling(n_simple)))

cat(sprintf("\n=== KEY DIFFERENCE ===\n"))
cat(sprintf("powerSurvEpi Freedman formula:\n"))
cat(sprintf("  m = (1/k)*((k*RR+1)/(RR-1))^2*(z_alpha+z_beta)^2\n"))
cat(sprintf("  n_E = m*k / (k*pE + pC)\n"))
cat(sprintf("  Result per group: %d\n", ceiling(n_E)))

cat(sprintf("\nSimplified Freedman formula (using average p):\n"))
cat(sprintf("  n = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / [p(1-p)(log(RR))^2]\n"))
cat(sprintf("  Result per group: %d\n", ceiling(n_simple)))

cat(sprintf("\nThe powerSurvEpi formula accounts for the unequal event probabilities\n"))
cat(sprintf("and uses a different parameterization based on relative risk,\n"))
cat(sprintf("NOT just the log hazard ratio.\n"))

# Two-sided log-rank test sample size: Freedman approximation
# powerSurvEpi::ssizeCT.default equivalent calculation

# Input parameters
alpha <- 0.05                  # two-sided significance level
power <- 0.80                  # target power
p_treatment <- 0.3707          # event probability in treatment arm
p_control <- 0.4890            # event probability in control arm
hr <- 0.7                      # hazard ratio
allocation_ratio <- 1          # 1:1 allocation

# Critical values
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)  # two-sided alpha cutoff
z_beta <- qnorm(power)         # one-sided power cutoff

# Overall (average) event probability
p <- (p_treatment + p_control) / 2

# Log hazard ratio
log_hr <- log(hr)

# Freedman approximation formula for per-group sample size
# n = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / [p(1-p)(log(HR))^2]
n_continuous <- (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / (p * (1 - p) * (log_hr)^2)

# Integer sample size (ceiling for per-group count)
n_integer <- ceiling(n_continuous)

cat("=== Freedman Approximation for Log-Rank Test (Two-sided) ===\n")
cat("\nInput Parameters:\n")
cat(sprintf("  Significance level (alpha):        %.4f\n", alpha))
cat(sprintf("  Target power:                      %.2f\n", power))
cat(sprintf("  Hazard ratio:                      %.2f\n", hr))
cat(sprintf("  Event probability (treatment):     %.4f\n", p_treatment))
cat(sprintf("  Event probability (control):       %.4f\n", p_control))
cat(sprintf("  Allocation ratio:                  1:1\n"))

cat("\nCalculation:\n")
cat(sprintf("  z_alpha (two-sided):               %.6f\n", z_alpha))
cat(sprintf("  z_beta (one-sided):                %.6f\n", z_beta))
cat(sprintf("  Average event probability (p):     %.6f\n", p))
cat(sprintf("  Log(hazard ratio):                 %.6f\n", log_hr))
cat(sprintf("  p(1-p):                            %.6f\n", p * (1 - p)))
cat(sprintf("  (log(HR))^2:                       %.6f\n", (log_hr)^2))

cat("\nResults:\n")
cat(sprintf("  Continuous sample size per group:  %.2f\n", n_continuous))
cat(sprintf("  Integer sample size per group:     %d\n", n_integer))
cat(sprintf("  Total sample size (both arms):     %d\n", 2 * n_integer))

# Store results for output
results <- list(
  metric = "sample_size",
  value = n_integer,
  unit = "participants_per_group",
  continuous_estimate = n_continuous
)

print(results)

     Sample size calculation for the Comparison of Survival Curves
     Between Two Groups under the Cox Proportional-Hazards Model for
     clinical trials.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     ssizeCT.default(power, 
                     k, 
                     pE, 
                     pC, 
                     RR, 
                     alpha = 0.05)
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

   power: numeric. power to detect the magnitude of the hazard ratio as
          small as that specified by ‘RR’.

       k: numeric. ratio of participants in group E (experimental
          group) compared to group C (control group).

      pE: numeric. probability of failure in group E (experimental
          group) over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      pC: numeric. probability of failure in group C (control group)
          over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      RR: numeric. postulated hazard ratio.

   alpha: numeric. type I error rate.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     This is an implementation of the sample size calculation method
     described in Section 14.12 (page 807) of Rosner (2006). The method
     was proposed by Freedman (1982).

     Suppose we want to compare the survival curves between an
     experimental group (E) and a control group (C) in a clinical trial
     with a maximum follow-up of t years.  The Cox proportional hazards
     regression model is assumed to have the form:

                      h(t|X_1)=h_0(t)\exp(beta_1 X_1).                  
     
     Let n_E be the number of participants in the E group and n_C be
     the number of participants in the C group.  We wish to test the
     hypothesis H0: RR=1 versus H1: RR not equal to 1, where
     RR=\exp(beta_1)=underlying hazard ratio for the E group versus the
     C group. Let RR be the postulated hazard ratio, alpha be the
     significance level. Assume that the test is a two-sided test. If
     the ratio of participants in group E compared to group C =
     n_E/n_C=k, then the number of participants needed in each group to
     achieve a power of 1-beta is

           n_E=\frac{m k}{k p_E + p_C}, n_C=\frac{m}{k p_E + p_C}

     z_{1-alpha/2}+z_{1-beta}

     standard normal distribution N(0, 1).

     element is n_C.

     n_C will be rounded up to integers.

# Investigate the Freedman formula implementation difference
# Let's understand what powerSurvEpi is doing vs our simple formula

library("powerSurvEpi")

# Re-create the Freedman formula as documented in powerSurvEpi help
# The documentation states:
# m = (1/k) * ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2 * (z_{1-alpha/2} + z_{1-beta})^2
# n_E = m*k / (k*p_E + p_C)
# n_C = m / (k*p_E + p_C)

power <- 0.80
k <- 1          # allocation ratio
pE <- 0.3707    # event prob experimental
pC <- 0.4890    # event prob control
RR <- 0.7       # hazard ratio (relative risk)
alpha <- 0.05

# Critical values
z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)    # two-sided
z_beta <- qnorm(power)              # one-sided

cat("=== Detailed Freedman Formula from powerSurvEpi Documentation ===\n\n")
cat(sprintf("Parameters:\n"))
cat(sprintf("  power = %.2f\n", power))
cat(sprintf("  k (allocation) = %.1f\n", k))
cat(sprintf("  pE = %.4f\n", pE))
cat(sprintf("  pC = %.4f\n", pC))
cat(sprintf("  RR = %.2f\n", RR))
cat(sprintf("  alpha = %.4f\n", alpha))

cat(sprintf("\nCritical values:\n"))
cat(sprintf("  z_{1-alpha/2} = %.6f\n", z_alpha_2))
cat(sprintf("  z_{1-beta} = %.6f\n", z_beta))
cat(sprintf("  z_{1-alpha/2} + z_{1-beta} = %.6f\n", z_alpha_2 + z_beta))

# Step 1: Calculate m
m_numerator <- (k * RR + 1)^2
m_denominator <- (RR - 1)^2
m_factor <- (1/k) * (m_numerator / m_denominator) * (z_alpha_2 + z_beta)^2

cat(sprintf("\nStep 1: Calculate m\n"))
cat(sprintf("  (k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1) = (%.1f*%.2f + 1)/(%.2f - 1) = (%.4f)/(%.4f) = %.6f\n",
    k, RR, RR, k*RR + 1, RR - 1, (k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1)))
cat(sprintf("  ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2 = %.6f\n", ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2))
cat(sprintf("  (1/k) * ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2 * (z_1-alpha/2 + z_1-beta)^2\n"))
cat(sprintf("  = (1/%.1f) * %.6f * %.6f\n", k, ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2, (z_alpha_2 + z_beta)^2))
cat(sprintf("  m = %.6f\n", m_factor))

# Step 2: Calculate n_E and n_C
denominator_common <- k * pE + pC

n_E <- m_factor * k / denominator_common
n_C <- m_factor / denominator_common

cat(sprintf("\nStep 2: Calculate sample sizes\n"))
cat(sprintf("  k*pE + pC = %.1f*%.4f + %.4f = %.6f\n", k, pE, pC, denominator_common))
cat(sprintf("  n_E = m*k / (k*pE + pC) = %.6f*%.1f / %.6f = %.6f → %d\n", 
    m_factor, k, denominator_common, n_E, ceiling(n_E)))
cat(sprintf("  n_C = m / (k*pE + pC) = %.6f / %.6f = %.6f → %d\n", 
    m_factor, denominator_common, n_C, ceiling(n_C)))

cat(sprintf("\n=== Comparison with Simple Formula ===\n"))
cat("Simple formula (what we used initially):\n")
cat("  n = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / [p(1-p)(log(RR))^2]\n")
cat("  where p = (pE + pC)/2\n")

p_avg <- (pE + pC) / 2
log_rr <- log(RR)
n_simple <- (z_alpha_2 + z_beta)^2 / (p_avg * (1 - p_avg) * (log_rr)^2)

cat(sprintf("\n  p_avg = (%.4f + %.4f)/2 = %.6f\n", pE, pC, p_avg))
cat(sprintf("  log(RR) = log(%.2f) = %.6f\n", RR, log_rr))
cat(sprintf("  n_simple = (%.6f)^2 / (%.6f * %.6f * (%.6f)^2)\n",
    z_alpha_2 + z_beta, p_avg, 1 - p_avg, log_rr))
cat(sprintf("  n_simple = %.6f → %d\n", n_simple, ceiling(n_simple)))

cat(sprintf("\n=== KEY DIFFERENCE ===\n"))
cat(sprintf("powerSurvEpi Freedman formula:\n"))
cat(sprintf("  m = (1/k)*((k*RR+1)/(RR-1))^2*(z_alpha+z_beta)^2\n"))
cat(sprintf("  n_E = m*k / (k*pE + pC)\n"))
cat(sprintf("  Result per group: %d\n", ceiling(n_E)))

cat(sprintf("\nSimplified Freedman formula (using average p):\n"))
cat(sprintf("  n = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / [p(1-p)(log(RR))^2]\n"))
cat(sprintf("  Result per group: %d\n", ceiling(n_simple)))

cat(sprintf("\nThe powerSurvEpi formula accounts for the unequal event probabilities\n"))
cat(sprintf("and uses a different parameterization based on relative risk,\n"))
cat(sprintf("NOT just the log hazard ratio.\n"))

# Two-sided log-rank test sample size: Freedman approximation
# powerSurvEpi::ssizeCT.default equivalent calculation

# Input parameters
alpha <- 0.05                  # two-sided significance level
power <- 0.80                  # target power
p_treatment <- 0.3707          # event probability in treatment arm
p_control <- 0.4890            # event probability in control arm
hr <- 0.7                      # hazard ratio
allocation_ratio <- 1          # 1:1 allocation

# Critical values
z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)  # two-sided alpha cutoff
z_beta <- qnorm(power)         # one-sided power cutoff

# Overall (average) event probability
p <- (p_treatment + p_control) / 2

# Log hazard ratio
log_hr <- log(hr)

# Freedman approximation formula for per-group sample size
# n = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / [p(1-p)(log(HR))^2]
n_continuous <- (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / (p * (1 - p) * (log_hr)^2)

# Integer sample size (ceiling for per-group count)
n_integer <- ceiling(n_continuous)

pC <- 0.4890    # event prob control
RR <- 0.7       # hazard ratio (relative risk)
alpha <- 0.05

# Critical values
z_alpha_2 <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)    # two-sided
z_beta <- qnorm(power)              # one-sided

cat("=== Detailed Freedman Formula from powerSurvEpi Documentation ===\n\n")
cat(sprintf("Parameters:\n"))
cat(sprintf("  power = %.2f\n", power))
cat(sprintf("  k (allocation) = %.1f\n", k))
cat(sprintf("  pE = %.4f\n", pE))
cat(sprintf("  pC = %.4f\n", pC))
cat(sprintf("  RR = %.2f\n", RR))
cat(sprintf("  alpha = %.4f\n", alpha))

cat(sprintf("\nCritical values:\n"))
cat(sprintf("  z_{1-alpha/2} = %.6f\n", z_alpha_2))
cat(sprintf("  z_{1-beta} = %.6f\n", z_beta))
cat(sprintf("  z_{1-alpha/2} + z_{1-beta} = %.6f\n", z_alpha_2 + z_beta))

# Step 1: Calculate m
m_numerator <- (k * RR + 1)^2
m_denominator <- (RR - 1)^2
m_factor <- (1/k) * (m_numerator / m_denominator) * (z_alpha_2 + z_beta)^2

cat(sprintf("\nStep 1: Calculate m\n"))
cat(sprintf("  (k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1) = (%.1f*%.2f + 1)/(%.2f - 1) = (%.4f)/(%.4f) = %.6f\n",
    k, RR, RR, k*RR + 1, RR - 1, (k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1)))
cat(sprintf("  ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2 = %.6f\n", ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2))
cat(sprintf("  (1/k) * ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2 * (z_1-alpha/2 + z_1-beta)^2\n"))
cat(sprintf("  = (1/%.1f) * %.6f * %.6f\n", k, ((k*RR + 1)/(RR - 1))^2, (z_alpha_2 + z_beta)^2))
cat(sprintf("  m = %.6f\n", m_factor))

# Step 2: Calculate n_E and n_C
denominator_common <- k * pE + pC

n_E <- m_factor * k / denominator_common
n_C <- m_factor / denominator_common

cat(sprintf("\nStep 2: Calculate sample sizes\n"))
cat(sprintf("  k*pE + pC = %.1f*%.4f + %.4f = %.6f\n", k, pE, pC, denominator_common))
cat(sprintf("  n_E = m*k / (k*pE + pC) = %.6f*%.1f / %.6f = %.6f → %d\n", 
    m_factor, k, denominator_common, n_E, ceiling(n_E)))
cat(sprintf("  n_C = m / (k*pE + pC) = %.6f / %.6f = %.6f → %d\n", 
    m_factor, denominator_common, n_C, ceiling(n_C)))

cat(sprintf("\n=== Comparison with Simple Formula ===\n"))
cat("Simple formula (what we used initially):\n")
cat("  n = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / [p(1-p)(log(RR))^2]\n")
cat("  where p = (pE + pC)/2\n")

p_avg <- (pE + pC) / 2
log_rr <- log(RR)
n_simple <- (z_alpha_2 + z_beta)^2 / (p_avg * (1 - p_avg) * (log_rr)^2)

cat(sprintf("\n  p_avg = (%.4f + %.4f)/2 = %.6f\n", pE, pC, p_avg))
cat(sprintf("  log(RR) = log(%.2f) = %.6f\n", RR, log_rr))
cat(sprintf("  n_simple = (%.6f)^2 / (%.6f * %.6f * (%.6f)^2)\n",
    z_alpha_2 + z_beta, p_avg, 1 - p_avg, log_rr))
cat(sprintf("  n_simple = %.6f → %d\n", n_simple, ceiling(n_simple)))

cat(sprintf("\n=== KEY DIFFERENCE ===\n"))
cat(sprintf("powerSurvEpi Freedman formula:\n"))
cat(sprintf("  m = (1/k)*((k*RR+1)/(RR-1))^2*(z_alpha+z_beta)^2\n"))
cat(sprintf("  n_E = m*k / (k*pE + pC)\n"))
cat(sprintf("  Result per group: %d\n", ceiling(n_E)))

cat(sprintf("\nSimplified Freedman formula (using average p):\n"))
cat(sprintf("  n = (z_alpha + z_beta)^2 / [p(1-p)(log(RR))^2]\n"))
cat(sprintf("  Result per group: %d\n", ceiling(n_simple)))

cat(sprintf("\nThe powerSurvEpi formula accounts for the unequal event probabilities\n"))
cat(sprintf("and uses a different parameterization based on relative risk,\n"))
cat(sprintf("NOT just the log hazard ratio.\n"))

# Evidence e6; success=true

# Final verification and reporting
library("powerSurvEpi")

result <- powerSurvEpi::ssizeCT.default(
  power = 0.80,
  k = 1,
  pE = 0.3707,
  pC = 0.4890,
  RR = 0.7,
  alpha = 0.05
)

cat("=== FINAL RESULT ===\n\n")
cat("Study Design: Two-arm, two-sided log-rank test\n")
cat("Method: Freedman (1982) approximation (as implemented in powerSurvEpi)\n")
cat("Reference: Rosner (2006) Example 14.42, page 809\n\n")

cat("Input Parameters:\n")
cat("  Type I error rate (α): 0.05 (two-sided)\n")
cat("  Target power: 0.80 (1 - β)\n")
cat("  Hazard ratio (RR): 0.70\n")
cat("  Event probability (experimental): 0.3707\n")
cat("  Event probability (control): 0.4890\n")
cat("  Allocation ratio (k): 1:1\n\n")

cat("Calculation (Full Freedman Formula):\n")
cat("  m = (1/k) × ((k×RR+1)/(RR-1))² × (z₁₋α/₂ + z₁₋β)²\n")
cat("  m = (1/1) × ((-5.667)²) × (2.802)² = 252.04\n")
cat("  n_E = m×k / (k×pE + pC) = 252.04 / 0.8597 = 293.17\n")
cat("  n_C = m / (k×pE + pC) = 252.04 / 0.8597 = 293.17\n\n")

cat("Results (rounded to integers):\n")
cat(sprintf("  Sample size per group: %d participants\n", result[1]))
cat(sprintf("  Total sample size: %d participants\n\n", result[1] + result[2]))

# Format output
POWER_AGENT_RESULT = jsonlite::toJSON(list(
  results = list(
    list(
      metric = "sample_size",
      value = as.integer(result[1]),
      unit = "participants_per_group"
    )
  )
), auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15)

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     Sample size calculation for the Comparison of Survival Curves
     Between Two Groups under the Cox Proportional-Hazards Model for
     clinical trials.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     ssizeCT.default(power, 
                     k, 
                     pE, 
                     pC, 
                     RR, 
                     alpha = 0.05)
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

   power: numeric. power to detect the magnitude of the hazard ratio as
          small as that specified by ‘RR’.

       k: numeric. ratio of participants in group E (experimental
          group) compared to group C (control group).

      pE: numeric. probability of failure in group E (experimental
          group) over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      pC: numeric. probability of failure in group C (control group)
          over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      RR: numeric. postulated hazard ratio.

   alpha: numeric. type I error rate.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     This is an implementation of the sample size calculation method
     described in Section 14.12 (page 807) of Rosner (2006). The method
     was proposed by Freedman (1982).

     Suppose we want to compare the survival curves between an
     experimental group (E) and a control group (C) in a clinical trial
     with a maximum follow-up of t years.  The Cox proportional hazards
     regression model is assumed to have the form:

                      h(t|X_1)=h_0(t)\exp(beta_1 X_1).                  
     
     Let n_E be the number of participants in the E group and n_C be
     the number of participants in the C group.  We wish to test the
     hypothesis H0: RR=1 versus H1: RR not equal to 1, where
     RR=\exp(beta_1)=underlying hazard ratio for the E group versus the
     C group. Let RR be the postulated hazard ratio, alpha be the
     significance level. Assume that the test is a two-sided test. If
     the ratio of participants in group E compared to group C =
     n_E/n_C=k, then the number of participants needed in each group to
     achieve a power of 1-beta is

           n_E=\frac{m k}{k p_E + p_C}, n_C=\frac{m}{k p_E + p_C}       
     
     where

     m=\frac{1}{k}<=ft(\frac{k RR + 1}{RR - 1}\right)^2<=ft(
     z_{1-alpha/2}+z_{1-beta}
     \right)^2,
     
     and z_{1-alpha/2} is the 100 (1-alpha/2)-th percentile of the
     standard normal distribution N(0, 1).

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

     A two-element vector. The first element is n_E and the second
     element is n_C.

_ N_ o_ t_ e:

     (1) The sample size formula assumes that the central-limit theorem
     is valid and hence is appropriate for large samples. (2) n_E and
     n_C will be rounded up to integers.

_ R_ e_ f_ e_ r_ e_ n_ c_ e_ s:

     in clinical trials using the log-rank test.  _Statistics in
     Medicine_. 1: 121-129

answer.method: Freedman approximation for log-rank test (powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default). The formula implements: power = Φ(√(k·m)·|RR-1|/(k·RR+1) - z_{1-α/2}), where k is the allocation ratio, m is the expected total number of events (nE·pE + nC·pC), RR is the hazard ratio, and z_{1-α/2} is the two-sided critical value from the standard normal distribution.
assumptions: Two-sided log-rank test at significance level α = 0.05

Hazard ratio (treatment vs control) = 0.7 under the alternative hypothesis
Event probabilities: pE = 0.3707 (treatment), pC = 0.4890 (control)
These event probabilities represent the marginal probability of event occurrence by the end of the follow-up period
Proportional hazards assumption holds
Independent observations within and across groups
Large-sample approximation via central-limit theorem is valid
limitations: The Freedman approximation is asymptotic and assumes large sample sizes; with expected events of 74.14 (treatment) and 97.8 (control), the approximation should be reasonable but may have small errors
Event probabilities are assumed known and fixed; in practice, they are estimated from preliminary data or literature and subject to sampling variability
The formula assumes proportional hazards, which should be verified in practice through diagnostic plots
Power is calculated assuming the alternative hypothesis (HR = 0.7) is true; the actual treatment effect may differ in practice

# Install and load powerSurvEpi package
if (!require("powerSurvEpi", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("powerSurvEpi")
}
library(powerSurvEpi)

# Parameters
n_treatment <- 200
n_control <- 200
total_n <- n_treatment + n_control
hazard_ratio <- 0.7
event_prob_treatment <- 0.3707
event_prob_control <- 0.4890
alpha <- 0.05
two_sided <- TRUE

# Calculate expected number of events
expected_events_treatment <- n_treatment * event_prob_treatment
expected_events_control <- n_control * event_prob_control
total_expected_events <- expected_events_treatment + expected_events_control

     This is an implementation of the power calculation method

     was proposed by Freedman (1982).

     experimental group (E) and a control group (C) in a clinical trial
     with a maximum follow-up of t years.  The Cox proportional hazards
     regression model is assumed to have the form:

     the number of participants in the C group.  We wish to test the
     hypothesis H0: RR=1 versus H1: RR not equal to 1, where
     RR=\exp(beta_1)=underlying hazard ratio for the E group versus the
     C group. Let RR be the postulated hazard ratio, alpha be the
     significance level. Assume that the test is a two-sided test. If
     the ratio of participants in group E compared to group C =

library(powerSurvEpi)

# Manual verification using Freedman formula
# Per the documentation:
# power = Phi(sqrt(k*m)*|RR-1|/(k*RR+1) - z_{1-alpha/2})
# where m = nE*pE + nC*pC and k = nE/nC

nE <- 200
nC <- 200
pE <- 0.3707
pC <- 0.4890
RR <- 0.7
alpha <- 0.05

# Calculate components
k <- nE / nC  # allocation ratio
m <- nE * pE + nC * pC  # total expected events
z_critical <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)  # two-sided critical value

# Freedman formula
numerator <- sqrt(k * m) * abs(RR - 1)
denominator <- k * RR + 1
z_statistic <- numerator / denominator - z_critical

# Power = Phi(z_statistic)
power_manual <- pnorm(z_statistic)

cat("Manual Verification of Freedman Formula\n")
cat("======================================\n\n")
cat("Formula: power = Φ(√(k·m)·|RR-1|/(k·RR+1) - z_{1-α/2})\n\n")
cat("Inputs:\n")
cat("- nE (treatment participants):", nE, "\n")
cat("- nC (control participants):", nC, "\n")
cat("- pE (event probability, treatment):", pE, "\n")
cat("- pC (event probability, control):", pC, "\n")
cat("- RR (hazard ratio):", RR, "\n")
cat("- alpha (significance level):", alpha, "\n\n")

cat("Intermediate calculations:\n")
cat("- k = nE/nC =", k, "\n")
cat("- m = nE·pE + nC·pC =", nE, "*", pE, "+", nC, "*", pC, "=", m, "\n")
cat("- z_{1-α/2} (two-sided critical value) =", z_critical, "\n")
cat("- √(k·m) =", sqrt(k * m), "\n")
cat("- |RR - 1| =", abs(RR - 1), "\n")
cat("- k·RR + 1 =", denominator, "\n\n")

cat("Freedman test statistic:\n")
cat("- √(k·m)·|RR-1|/(k·RR+1) =", numerator / denominator, "\n")
cat("- z_statistic = √(k·m)·|RR-1|/(k·RR+1) - z_{1-α/2} =", z_statistic, "\n\n")

cat("Power calculations:\n")
cat("- Manual (via formula): Φ(", z_statistic, ") =", power_manual, "\n")

# Compare with powerCT.default
power_function <- powerCT.default(nE = nE, nC = nC, pE = pE, pC = pC, RR = RR, alpha = alpha)
cat("- powerCT.default result:", power_function, "\n")
cat("- Difference:", abs(power_manual - power_function), "\n")

cat("\n✓ Calculations match\n")

library(powerSurvEpi)

# Manual verification using Freedman formula
# Per the documentation:
# power = Phi(sqrt(k*m)*|RR-1|/(k*RR+1) - z_{1-alpha/2})
# where m = nE*pE + nC*pC and k = nE/nC

nE <- 200
nC <- 200
pE <- 0.3707
pC <- 0.4890
RR <- 0.7
alpha <- 0.05

# Calculate components
k <- nE / nC  # allocation ratio
m <- nE * pE + nC * pC  # total expected events
z_critical <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)  # two-sided critical value

# Freedman formula
numerator <- sqrt(k * m) * abs(RR - 1)
denominator <- k * RR + 1
z_statistic <- numerator / denominator - z_critical

# Power = Phi(z_statistic)
power_manual <- pnorm(z_statistic)

cat("Manual Verification of Freedman Formula\n")
cat("======================================\n\n")
cat("Formula: power = Φ(√(k·m)·|RR-1|/(k·RR+1) - z_{1-α/2})\n\n")
cat("Inputs:\n")
cat("- nE (treatment participants):", nE, "\n")
cat("- nC (control participants):", nC, "\n")
cat("- pE (event probability, treatment):", pE, "\n")
cat("- pC (event probability, control):", pC, "\n")
cat("- RR (hazard ratio):", RR, "\n")
cat("- alpha (significance level):", alpha, "\n\n")

cat("Intermediate calculations:\n")
cat("- k = nE/nC =", k, "\n")
cat("- m = nE·pE + nC·pC =", nE, "*", pE, "+", nC, "*", pC, "=", m, "\n")
cat("- z_{1-α/2} (two-sided critical value) =", z_critical, "\n")
cat("- √(k·m) =", sqrt(k * m), "\n")
cat("- |RR - 1| =", abs(RR - 1), "\n")
cat("- k·RR + 1 =", denominator, "\n\n")

cat("Freedman test statistic:\n")
cat("- √(k·m)·|RR-1|/(k·RR+1) =", numerator / denominator, "\n")
cat("- z_statistic = √(k·m)·|RR-1|/(k·RR+1) - z_{1-α/2} =", z_statistic, "\n\n")

cat("Power calculations:\n")
cat("- Manual (via formula): Φ(", z_statistic, ") =", power_manual, "\n")

power_function <- powerCT.default(nE = nE, nC = nC, pE = pE, pC = pC, RR = RR, alpha = alpha)
cat("- powerCT.default result:", power_function, "\n")
cat("- Difference:", abs(power_manual - power_function), "\n")
